item.title: Nearly 9 in 10 Americans report widespread government corruption after Trump's return
item.description:
Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Americans' perceptions of government corruption have hit a 20-year high following President Trump's return to office, a new Gallup survey found.

Why it matters: The results signal a deepening crisis of confidence in the federal government as trust in U.S. institutions already hovers near an all-time low.

By the numbers: 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread, Gallup found.

  • That's a 10-point increase from last year and well above the 72%–79% range between 2010 and 2025.

Democrats are driving most of the rise, jumping to 91% this year after sitting at 76% during the first year of Trump's term.

  • In 2024, when President Biden was still in office, 57% of Democrats said government corruption was widespread.
  • About 90% of independents think corruption is widespread, up 12 points since 2024.

Between the lines: Trump raked in more than $2.2 billion in the first year of his second term.

  • In 2024, he reported making about $600 million. A substantial share of Trump's income comes from non-traditional business holdings, like his cryptocurrency business.
  • He faced criticism after an investment firm tied to the United Arab Emirates bought almost half of his main crypto firm, prmopting accusations of potential foreign influence over U.S. policy.
  • He's also making money from a new plan to offer early access to his Truth Social posts, which can move markets.

Zoom out: Congressional lawmakers have repeatedly called out what they say are conflicts of interests.

  • Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) released a report in November that concluded Trump and his family significantly benefitted from rolling back crypto regulations designed to protect Americans from fraud and scams.
  • Democrats have also criticized the president for accepting lavish gifts, including a $400 million Qatari jet.
  • It's also not just the president — congressional lawmakers have faced growing scrutiny for making head-turning sums trading stocks while in office.

What they're saying: "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement.

  • "The Democrats in Congress have refused to do anything to stop waste, fraud, and abuse in our government."

Zoom in: Republicans have held a much steadier view of government corruption.

  • About eight in 10 say corruption is widespread, relatively on par with 2024 levels, when 87% said the same.
  • Republicans' consistent reading suggests this feeling is widespread regardless of which political party is in power.

The big picture: While citizens in many developed nations feel their governments are becoming less corrupt, Americans are experiencing the exact opposite trend.

  • Among the 38 member countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the median level of perceived government corruption has fallen from 69% in 2009 to below 60% since 2022.
  • For the first time ever, the U.S. now tops perceived corruption ratings by comparison to the other countries in the OECD. Since 2023, just four other countries that Gallup has surveyed have scored higher than the U.S., including Lebanon, Peru, Ghana and Nigeria.
  • The data for 2026 isn't complete because Gallup conducts their polling on a country-by-country basis over the year, so that massive gap could grow wider this year.

Methodology: Gallup surveyed at least 1,000 Americans every year since 2005 to reach these results. It also surveyed between 500 and more than 3,000 people in other countries to measure sentiment across the other OECD countries. Go deeper: Trump's profits irk Americans as Dems test anti-corruption message
item.content:encoded:
Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Americans' perceptions of government corruption have hit a 20-year high following President Trump's return to office, a new Gallup survey found.

Why it matters: The results signal a deepening crisis of confidence in the federal government as trust in U.S. institutions already hovers near an all-time low.

By the numbers: 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread, Gallup found.

  • That's a 10-point increase from last year and well above the 72%–79% range between 2010 and 2025.

Democrats are driving most of the rise, jumping to 91% this year after sitting at 76% during the first year of Trump's term.

  • In 2024, when President Biden was still in office, 57% of Democrats said government corruption was widespread.
  • About 90% of independents think corruption is widespread, up 12 points since 2024.

Between the lines: Trump raked in more than $2.2 billion in the first year of his second term.

  • In 2024, he reported making about $600 million. A substantial share of Trump's income comes from non-traditional business holdings, like his cryptocurrency business.
  • He faced criticism after an investment firm tied to the United Arab Emirates bought almost half of his main crypto firm, prmopting accusations of potential foreign influence over U.S. policy.
  • He's also making money from a new plan to offer early access to his Truth Social posts, which can move markets.

Zoom out: Congressional lawmakers have repeatedly called out what they say are conflicts of interests.

  • Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) released a report in November that concluded Trump and his family significantly benefitted from rolling back crypto regulations designed to protect Americans from fraud and scams.
  • Democrats have also criticized the president for accepting lavish gifts, including a $400 million Qatari jet.
  • It's also not just the president — congressional lawmakers have faced growing scrutiny for making head-turning sums trading stocks while in office.

What they're saying: "President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in an emailed statement.

  • "The Democrats in Congress have refused to do anything to stop waste, fraud, and abuse in our government."

Zoom in: Republicans have held a much steadier view of government corruption.

  • About eight in 10 say corruption is widespread, relatively on par with 2024 levels, when 87% said the same.
  • Republicans' consistent reading suggests this feeling is widespread regardless of which political party is in power.

The big picture: While citizens in many developed nations feel their governments are becoming less corrupt, Americans are experiencing the exact opposite trend.

  • Among the 38 member countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the median level of perceived government corruption has fallen from 69% in 2009 to below 60% since 2022.
  • For the first time ever, the U.S. now tops perceived corruption ratings by comparison to the other countries in the OECD. Since 2023, just four other countries that Gallup has surveyed have scored higher than the U.S., including Lebanon, Peru, Ghana and Nigeria.
  • The data for 2026 isn't complete because Gallup conducts their polling on a country-by-country basis over the year, so that massive gap could grow wider this year.

Methodology: Gallup surveyed at least 1,000 Americans every year since 2005 to reach these results. It also surveyed between 500 and more than 3,000 people in other countries to measure sentiment across the other OECD countries. item.title: Lutnick: Anthropic is "back on the right side" with Trump administration
item.description:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the Trump administration now trusts Anthropic following months of clashes with the AI company.

Why it matters: The statement marks a remarkable turnaround in a relationship strained by a bitter fight over national security and AI safeguards.

What they're saying: Asked if he trusts Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Lutnick told Axios' Mike Allen: "We trust Anthropic."

  • "They've done what we asked. They're back on the right side. So the answer is: Yes," Lutnick said in an interview on Tuesday.

The big picture: The declaration comes as Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown takes a more prominent role in the company's relationship with the White House, including a headlining spot at this week's G20 Innovation Ministerial.

  • "Really excited for our conversation, so I'd like to introduce you all to Tom Brown, one of the founders of Anthropic," Lutnick said on Wednesday to a room full of G20 ministers.
  • Lutnick kicked off the discussion offering Brown an opportunity to introduce himself to an international audience: "I don't think they know you so well. Anthropic, of course, is famous, but a little story helps."

What they're saying: Brown praised President Trump's pro-data center post on Truth Social this week.

  • "I really love Trump's post from earlier this week... where he was pointing out that the data centers are just an enormous source of prosperity," Brown said.
  • "They produce a ton of jobs. They produce taxes. Now the way that we design them, we actually bring on more power to the grid," he said.
  • Brown also highlighted Anthropic's support for the administration's ratepayer pledge.

Between the lines: Industry knows aligning with the Trump administration goes a long way for policy priorities.

Catch up quick: Personality differences added fuel to the fire in a clash between the Trump administration and Anthropic earlier this year that resulted in sweeping export controls on the company's most advanced models.

  • Brown was instrumental in patching up the relationship, holding multiple conversations with Lutnick and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross.
  • A federal judge in August, meanwhile, struck down the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk, ruling that the government's actions violated Anthropic's constitutional rights.
  • The company is also fighting a separate Pentagon designation under a different statute in the D.C. Circuit.

The bottom line: Brown offers a reset for a company once on the outs with the White House.

item.title: After Trump renamed Lake Ontario, Americans aren't buying his Canada fight
item.description:
President Trump's order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America" isn't floating with Americans, with a majority opposing the name change and his new tariffs on Washington's northern neighbor, per recent polling.

The big picture: After trade talks between the longtime allies collapsed last month and triggered steep new tariffs, the Trump administration has escalated its feud with Canada.

  • With the midterm elections creeping closer, polling suggests Americans aren't sold on the fight.

Driving the news: Reuters-Ipsos polling from late August found that more than 6 in 10 (63%) of Americans oppose Trump's executive order directing Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to rename the lake, which straddles the U.S.–Canada border.

  • Even among Republicans, more opposed (43%) than supported (33%) the order.
  • A vast majority of Democrats (84%) and independents and other parties (65%) opposed the name change.

The other side: In response to the polling, the White House lambasted Canada in a statement to Axios.

  • "Canada has been a bad neighbor by ripping off our country for years," wrote spokesperson Taylor Rogers. "President Trump promised voters that he would not allow our country to be taken advantage of anymore, which is why he is fighting so hard to protect American industries and workers."

Zoom out: An Economist–YouGov survey of 1,592 U.S. citizens similarly found that 68% oppose changing the lake's name — a sentiment shared by 43% of 2024 Trump voters.

  • Just 36% of Trump voters approve.

Friction point: Despite the opposition, Apple and Google both changed their map labels on the body of water — for U.S. users, at least.

  • Google said it did so to match updates from the U.S. Geographic Names Information System. The company's statement said those in Canada will continue to see "Lake Ontario," while the rest of the world will see both names.
  • Apple made the switch after Trump personally appealed to the tech giant, Burgum told Fox Business earlier this week.

Zoom out: Trump's new tariffs on Canada are also unpopular: 57% oppose them, while just 20% support them, and 21% aren't sure.

  • Canada is set to retaliate against the new 50% U.S. tariff on some $20 billion of Canadian goods.
  • Democrats (82%) and independents (59%) oppose the levies. More Republicans support the tariffs than oppose them (44% v. 33%), but 22% say they don't know how they feel.

The bottom line: On social media and in trade policy, the Trump administration isn't showing signs of backing off of its quarrel with Canada.

  • But if you ask Americans, more say it's America who's responsible for the trade war (46%) than Canada (12%). Plus, just 4% say it will have a positive impact on their personal finances.

The fine print: Ipsos surveyed a nationally representative sample of 1,023 adults between Aug. 28-30, 2026. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.5 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.

Go deeper: Scoop: Dems plan bill to counter Trump's "Lake America" order

item.title: America is seeing an uptick in executions
item.description:
Data: Death Penalty Information Center; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

Florida executed its 14th prisoner for the year on Tuesday, adding to a post-COVID surge in capital punishment that drove more executions last year than any since 2009.

The big picture: Even as fewer courts sentence defendants to death and more than half of the states have banned or at least temporarily halted the practice, the Trump administration has overtly cheered on the death penalty.

  • "The increased number of executions last year reflected the enthusiasm and the urging of this administration to increase use of the death penalty, and the acquiescence of some state officials to that political pressure," Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher tells Axios.

By the numbers: Forty-seven people were executed last year, 19 of whom were in Florida, according to the DPI's database dating back to 1977.

  • 2026 is falling behind that pace. Twenty-four people have been executed this year, with more than a dozen still scheduled.

Zoom in: Florida has led the way with executions, including two men being put to death within hours of one another back in July. It was the first time the state had done so in more than six decades.

  • Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has signed death warrants at a rapid pace, setting off the spree at a level unseen in decades.
  • "I think we'll probably end up having done more [executions] than any administration in the history of the state of Florida," he said in July, adding, "I'm not like taking any pride in that, because it's a weighty thing."

Catch up quick: While there has not been a federal execution since 2021, President Trump signed a day-one executive order instructing his attorney general to pursue the death penalty and ensure states have a sufficient supply of drugs for lethal injections.

  • His approach was a sharp departure from the Biden administration, which imposed a moratorium on federal capital punishment amid a DOJ review and commuted the sentences for 37 of the 40 people on federal death row.
  • Trump, on the other hand, oversaw a historic use of capital punishment in his first term, with 13 executions in roughly six months. Currently, only three people are on federal death row, none of whom have exhausted their appeals, Maher explains.
  • While Trump's DOJ has pushed to authorize new federal capital cases, none have gone to trial, she adds.

Yes, but: DPI's data doesn't point to a wave of executions that could rival '90s or 2000s levels. Fewer than 25 people were sentenced to death in 2025 per DPI's tracker, compared to numbers well into the 100s in the 2000s.

  • "The majority of capital juries are imposing life sentences, not death sentences," Maher says, adding she's doubtful the country will ever return to the high numbers of executions in the '90s and 2000s.

Friction point: That aligns with slipping public support for the death penalty, per Gallup's trend, which hit its lowest level since 1972 (52%) last year.

  • But Pew Research Center polling from July found that about two-thirds of Americans (66%) favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder, up from 60% in April 2021. Still, a majority (59%) say the death penalty is not a crime deterrent.
  • "The realization in the public that the system is getting it wrong quite often has really influenced public opinion and has affected the support for the death penalty," Maher says, noting that since 1973, more than 200 former death-row pris­on­ers have been exon­er­at­ed due to wrongful convictions.

What we're watching: Florida is set to add to its tally again, with an execution set for September 10.

Go deeper: How the death penalty works

item.title: Like "pissing in the wind": Local concerns bulldozed by Trump's border wall plan
item.description:
The Trump administration has a blunt message for state and local officials trying to prevent construction of a wall and other security measures along the 2,000-mile southern border: Resistance is futile.

Driving the news: President Trump's envoys recently met privately with officials from Texas border counties where residents have pushed back against construction, saying the plans are unnecessary in rugged landscapes with few immigrant crossings and that they'd harm the environment.

  • The officials were told bluntly at the closed-door meeting with Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott that there would be no negotiating.
  • The government is now pushing ahead with plans to build hundreds more miles of the 30-foot, steel barrier in most counties, and says there will be vehicle barriers and other construction in the Big Bend state and national parks.
  • "It is like my dad would say, it's sort of like pissing in the wind. You just, you know, it just ain't right, folks. This is completely asinine," Val Verde County Judge Lewis Owens said in a video statement about the meeting with the federal officials.

Zoom in: Scott told local officials that wall construction along a more than 200-mile stretch from Hudspeth County to Presidio County was "not negotiable" without giving a reason, Brewster County Sheriff Ronny Dodson, who was at the meeting, told Axios.

  • County sheriffs and judges, the top elected officials in rural Texas counties, have been the only ones invited to make their case to Scott while he temporarily paused construction.
  • Private landowners, ranch owners and eco-tourism business owners who will be impacted by any construction weren't invited to the meeting.
  • "The people making the decisions above Commissioner Scott, they've never been down here," Owens said. "They don't know what the hell this place looks like, but yet you're making decisions on what's going to affect us that live here."

At the meeting, Scott acknowledged a lack of transparency by the federal government on construction plans so far, Dodson said.

  • "They just paused for a couple of weeks and we are where we were before," said Susan Hays, who's running for a Presidio County commissioner's seat. She wasn't invited to the meeting but was given details by the county judge.

The latest: A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order pausing construction over the roughly 600 miles of border, but that order lasts only through the end of this month.

  • Significant construction on private land is likely to be delayed — for now, at least.
  • Only about 20 % of landowners in Presidio County, west of the state park, have signed away land access to the feds, while only about 31 % of landowners east of the park have, Deirdre Hisler, a Presidio County commissioner, told Axios.
  • U.S. officials have made clear that landowners who don't comply risk an eminent domain lawsuit over their property.

What they're saying: "We are currently evaluating technology options to meet President Trump's mission of zero illegal border crossings while strengthening the most secure border in American history in highly remote and hard-to-access areas," a CBP spokesperson said in a statement.

The intrigue: Federal officials are giving Brewster County, home to much of the Big Bend national and state parks as well as the Black Gap Wildlife Management area, some room to negotiate.

  • These areas aren't slated to have a 30-foot wall, but construction for planned patrol roads and vehicle barriers have alarmed locals who want to protect the parks' environment and its eco-tourism industry.

Dodson said he's been taking local CBP officials on site visits to try to persuade them from building a new road through the parks and limit the number of vehicle barriers CBP plans.

  • "This county is concerned about tourism, and you may hear that word a lot," Dodson said. "But there's a lot of truth there because we don't have oil or gas or anything. We don't have much."
  • He added that "the stuff that people are saying on Facebook, — 'Oh this wall, wall, wall, wall' — it's already scaring people off because our tourism is down right now."

The big picture: The pressure on local officials in the Big Bend area to submit to the construction plans is part of a pattern for CBP, which had built less than 200 miles of border wall as of last week.

  • It recently started construction in Tohono O'odham Nation territory in Arizona, though the tribe has gone to court to try to stop the work.
  • Even religious sites aren't being spared from eminent domain lawsuits and major construction.

item.title: How AI is playing a growing role in wildfire response
item.description:
AI is already helping detect and monitor wildfires. Now, researchers are exploring how it could help fire officials decide where to deploy crews across multiple fires.

Why it matters: Studies show climate change is contributing to longer, more intense wildfire seasons, forcing officials to make high-stakes decisions about how to prioritize limited resources. AI could help them process information to make those decisions faster.

State of play: Jason Fallon, the U.S. Wildland Fire Service's division chief for wildland fire intelligence, told Axios that AI is ingrained in many areas of wildfire management nationally, including monitoring, detection, information dissemination and data transfer.

  • AI-powered cameras, satellite systems and weather-prediction tools are helping agencies in Western states detect wildfires and deploy crews sooner.
  • For satellite data triage, AI can "help us quickly work through a workflow to separate noise from reality," Fallon said.

Zoom in: Léonard Boussioux, an information systems professor at the University of Washington Foster School of Business, is part of a team researching how machine learning and optimization could assist fire officials in deciding where to send crews when multiple wildfires are burning.

  • The approach predicts how multiple fires could evolve under different levels of suppression, then uses a mathematical model to recommend how crews could be deployed, according to a research paper that has yet to be peer reviewed.

By the numbers: Last year, 77,850 wildfires were recorded across the U.S. — "noticeably higher than the five- and 10-year averages," according to the National Interagency Coordination Center.

  • This year's wildfire season is surpassing the 10-year average for the number of fires and acres burned, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

What they're saying: "What's hard to do is to predict which fire is going to blow up," Boussioux told Axios.

  • "Which fire should we prioritize right now, knowing that we don't necessarily have [the] resources?"
  • Boussioux's team is trying to anticipate how multiple fires could evolve simultaneously.
  • "What we are doing essentially is: We predict two weeks in advance, and we also predict how [multiple fires] will behave" under different levels of suppression, Boussioux said.

What we're watching: Fallon said that research like Boussioux's has potential to aid wildfire decision-making, but "I don't think we know yet to what degree."

Reality check: AI's role is to augment firefighters, decision-makers and analysts — not replace them, Fallon said. Fire officials remain "in control of directing the strategy and action," he said.

  • AI can reduce cognitive workload and accelerate insights in complex, fast-changing environments, he said, but expertise, experience and risk decisions still need to come from humans.
  • "The machine doesn't have 30 years of experience fighting fire," he said.
  • A model might not know that residents at the end of a road don't have vehicles and need assistance during an evacuation. "It only knows what we can provide to it," Fallon said.

Between the lines: AI won't solve the problem of massive, destructive wildfires, Matt Weiner, CEO of Megafire Action, a nonprofit focused on reducing catastrophic wildfire risk, told Axios.

  • "What it can do, and what it's already showing that it can do, is help us prioritize where we can do the most efficient work at every scale," Weiner said.
  • That could mean helping fire officials understand how a new wildfire is likely to behave so they can "direct the right resources for the right fire," he said.
  • AI can provide inaccurate information, potentially putting lives and property at risk, while limited data on rare events can hinder its ability to forecast extreme wildfires, according to the Government Accountability Office.

What's next: Researchers are developing more sophisticated tools for modeling complicated wildfire decisions, but their usefulness will depend on the quality and organization of the underlying data.

  • "We already have technology to make things better, but we do not necessarily have data available, or it's not properly managed or organized," Boussioux said.

Amy Harder contributed reporting.

item.title: OpenAI, Anthropic aim to balance safety, progress as IPOs near
item.description:
OpenAI and Anthropic are trying to strike a delicate balance: convincing Wall Street that their businesses are sound and fast-growing, while at the same time assuring governments and the world that their models don't pose unacceptable risks.

Why it matters: Both companies are aiming for potentially record-breaking initial public offerings soon.

Driving the news: OpenAI on Tuesday said it will soon release its Astra model broadly, but said the model has reached a "critical" cybersecurity threshold and that its most powerful capabilities in that area will be initially limited to trusted testers.

  • Anthropic, meanwhile, debuted updated versions of its latest Fable and Mythos releases designed to address key criticisms of the initial release, including concerns around cost, data sharing and a model too keen to refuse legitimate requests.

Zoom in: OpenAI warned that Astra's safeguards may mistakenly flag legitimate activity as cyber misuse or unauthorized behavior, and this could slow, pause or stop users' tasks.

  • Meanwhile, Anthropic said its new models are less likely to trigger safeguards that route them to more restricted responses.
  • Medical or biology questions will have 85% fewer interventions, while some users could see roughly 60% fewer cybersecurity-related interventions per session, Anthropic said.

The big picture: Anthropic could file a publicly available prospectus as soon as next week, while OpenAI is in earlier stages of its IPO process.

The intrigue: Anthropic is striking a commercially friendly note with its release while OpenAI is sounding more sober on the safety front.

  • In addition to limiting the release of Astra, OpenAI's head of strategic futures, Dean Ball, penned an essay on how the Hugging Face incident is likely only the beginning of AI systems escaping human containment measures, with future agents seeking to become "sovereign" from human control.
  • "They will pay their own bills for the compute they run on," he predicted. "If they answer to humans at all, they will only do so partially, for example by providing services to humans in exchange for pay."

With the new release, Anthropic is updating its risk classifiers to reduce refusals of safe prompts, a key criticism of the earlier version.

  • Anthropic also debuted a system — very similar in approach to one OpenAI recently previewed — designed to ensure it can monitor the safety of enterprise model use without needing to store customer data, as it initially had required.

What we're watching: Expect both companies' public statements to vacillate between optimistic and cautious.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic are trying to simultaneously convince investors that their growth opportunity justifies unprecedented expenses and valuations while also assuring regulators in D.C. and elsewhere that they're being prudent.

Editor's note: This story has been corrected to reflect  that Anthropic says its attempts to reduce refusals of safe prompts involve updating its risk classifiers (not dialing back safeguards).

item.title: Trump's AI team fractures over strategy against G20 backdrop
item.description:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — Trump administration officials came to this week's G20 innovation summit to project a united front on U.S. AI leadership. But tensions between the Commerce Department and the White House's tech policy shop are playing out behind the scenes.

Why it matters: The Trump administration wants the world to follow its lead on AI policy, even as it grapples with divisions at home.

Driving the news: The G20 Innovation Ministerial on Tuesday and Wednesday features some of the tech industry's heaviest hitters and officials from the world's most powerful countries.

  • Officials and executives pitched the U.S. as a model for other countries on AI, contrasting its lighter regulatory approach with the European Union's heavier hand.
  • White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios credited U.S. AI progress to "flexible policy frameworks" that encourage private investment and provide regulatory clarity.

The intrigue: The Commerce Department and OSTP are jockeying for influence over the administration's AI policy agenda. Key regulatory decisions remain unsettled as the U.S. tries to present a clear message abroad.

  • "This is fake news," a White House spokesperson told Axios. "The President's team is working closely together to showcase American leadership on the world stage as this year's G20 hosts."
  • "Commerce and OSTP are jointly leading a productive and successful G20 Innovation Summit."

Behind the scenes: The summit's first day highlighted the divide between OSTP and Commerce, including how they view each other and an apparent messaging miscue over data centers.

  • Commerce holds many of the administration's most important AI policy levers, including the Bureau of Industry and Security and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation.
  • A source familiar with the administration's thinking described OSTP as a shop of "thinkers" without the regulatory authorities wielded by Commerce.
  • The divide was also visible in the summit's programming: Kratsios spearheaded Tuesday's agenda, speaking virtually with Elon Musk, Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.
  • Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will take center stage on Wednesday, hosting fireside chats with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown and Palantir CEO Alex Karp.

In an interview with Axios' Mike Allen, Lutnick emphasized that his guests will appear in person.

  • "I tried to bring deeply interesting people, but only in person," Lutnick told Axios.
  • "Everybody offers to come on video. But come on! If you're not gonna get on the plane and come and join where the top 20 countries of the world are, that's OK."

"We're one team," Kratsios told reporters on Tuesday.

  • A source familiar with the administration's thinking said Musk would have made the trip had there been better coordination leading up to the summit. Another source disputed that characterization, saying that Musk had been confirmed as a virtual participant for three weeks and his team consistently opted for that format.

Tension point: The apparent lack of coordination between OSTP and Commerce spilled into the summit's messaging on data centers, a fraught political issue for the administration.

  • Kratsios raised data centers during his chat with Musk, despite plans to avoid the topic at the summit following President Trump's "let Data Reign" Truth Social post, a source familiar with the administration's thinking said.
  • The source said officials wanted to avoid the issue because it has become a midterm flashpoint and Chinese representatives were in the audience.
  • Kratsios later echoed Trump's position, telling reporters that data centers are ultimately a "community decision" that can bring local benefits if providers supply their own power.

The big picture: The U.S. is pushing other countries to hold off on AI regulation, even as the Trump administration debates its own approach to overseeing the most advanced models.

  • The White House has finalized but not publicly released a framework for reviewing some frontier models before deployment.
  • The administration is still debating key pieces of its approach to AI regulation, including a proposed FINRA-like regulatory body for AI, and a replacement for former President Biden's AI diffusion rule governing the export of advanced AI chips and models.

What they're saying: Leading up to the summit, a White House official told Reuters that "the U.S. will ​press member countries not to set ​up new regulatory organizations to oversee ⁠AI development."

  • David Sacks, an outside adviser to Trump on AI, said he opposed the creation of a new regulatory body for AI. "There's already, I think, a thicket of laws that apply to AI," Sacks said in his virtual address to G20 ministers.

The bottom line: The future of AI regulation on a global scale is playing out amid D.C. power struggles.

item.title: Rogue House Democrats Golden and Perez face growing push for "consequences"
item.description:
Two centrist House Democrats who voted to help Republicans get a procedural motion across the finish line are now facing down possible punishment from party leaders who say they were blindsided by the move.

Why it matters: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is taking an uncharacteristically aggressive public approach to the defections, to the thrill of some of his members.

  • "I 'effing love it," said Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.). "We have to draw a bright line here and kick some ass or this will be the new norm."
  • Another House Democrat said Jeffries and his deputies "are right to make an example" of the two rogue centrists.

Catch up quick: Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) voted with Republicans to pass what is called a "rule" — a procedural measure that sets the terms for House debate on a package of bills.

  • While lawmakers often break away from party leaders on standard legislative votes on legislation, these procedural votes almost always fall along party lines.
  • The legislation advanced by the measure included a Republican resolution denouncing "socialism in all its forms," which infuriated many Democrats because it also included language praising the GOP's SAVE America Act.

What they're saying: Jeffries, in a joint statement with Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) and Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) released Tuesday night, signaled plans to take action.

  • "The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic Caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust," the trio said.
  • "It is an action that necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order."

The other side: Golden defended his vote by noting that the rule also contained a bill he co-authored to shield lobstermen from federal regulations protecting whales.

  • Golden argued that leadership should not have been surprised by his vote and that his intentions were neither veiled nor unpredictable, telling Axios: "They couldn't possibly think I would vote against my own bill, right?"
  • Gluesenkamp Perez also cited Golden's bill protecting lobstermen as the reason for her vote in a statement.
  • Neither office immediately responded to requests for comment on the joint leadership statement.

What we're hearing: A "general conversation about consequences" sprang up among members almost immediately after the vote on Tuesday, a second House Democrat, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told Axios.

  • The lawmaker said that while only "a few people" explicitly raised the idea of punishment, the "sentiment is wider spread."
  • Democratic leadership is "upset that they put all of the front liners in the position to take hard votes. Very upset," said a third House Democrat.
  • Several lawmakers told Axios that one idea being circulated is stripping Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez of their committee assignments.

Between the lines: Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez are facing intense anger from colleagues, who feel they snatched a potential win from the party with just a few months until the November midterm elections.

  • "Golden and MGP not only broke trust with our leadership and the caucus writ-large, it was also a deeply selfish act," said the first House Democrat.
  • "They threw their frontline and other colleagues under the bus. There are votes that could have been avoided had the rule failed that members will now have to take a vote on."

Reality check: Even members who are furious with Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez acknowledge any action would likely be symbolic and, could, in the case of the latter, backfire politically.

  • Golden is retiring come Jan. 3, while Gluesenkamp Perez is running for reelection in one of the most Republican-leaning House districts held by a Democrat.
  • A moderate House Democrat also told Axios that the action outlined in Jeffries' statement represents a "pretty strong response" and "thus needs to be consistent and dished out accordingly to all factions of caucus."

Between the lines: While Jeffries and Clark were together on the joint statement, sources said there was significant tension between their offices in the immediate aftermath of Tuesday's vote.

  • Jeffries' initial reaction to the vote was to point to Clark, whose job is to get members in line on votes, telling reporters, "You'll have to talk to Katherine."
  • A Clark spokesperson stressed that, like Jeffries, Clark did not get a heads-up about how Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez planned to vote.

The bottom line: "I think if you throw all of your colleagues under the bus by voting with the other party on a procedural rule vote, you should lose your committee assignments and get reassigned to the arts and crafts committee," said Huffman.

item.title: Pentagon turmoil deepens as Hegseth consolidates control
item.description:
The Pentagon has entered a period of profound institutional turmoil, as a crisis of leadership at home converges with a crisis of capacity abroad.

Why it matters: Six months into the Iran war, Pete Hegseth presides over a Pentagon with fewer senior leaders, fewer critical weapons and less public accountability than at any point in President Trump's two terms.

Zoom in: The most striking departure yet came Monday from Army Secretary Dan Driscoll — Vice President Vance's close friend and Yale Law classmate, once viewed as a potential successor to Hegseth himself.

  • Driscoll, a rising star whom Trump had tapped for sensitive diplomacy in Ukraine, resigned after months of clashes with Hegseth over the Army's leadership and modernization.
  • His exit, following Hegseth's firing of Army chief Gen. Randy George, leaves the service without Senate-confirmed civilian or uniformed leadership in the midst of the Iran war.

Zoom out: Hegseth has fired or forced out senior officers across nearly every service, including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, the Navy's top admiral and the Army chief of staff.

  • The Washington Post counts more than two dozen top officers dismissed under Hegseth, who has remade nearly the entire Joint Chiefs. Only the Marine Corps and Space Force chiefs he inherited are still serving.
  • The New York Times reports that Hegseth has also personally removed at least 45 officers from promotion lists this year — an extraordinary intervention in a system traditionally insulated from political leadership.
  • NBC News reported Tuesday that Hegseth has blocked more promotions in recent weeks, including more than a dozen Black, Hispanic or female officers across the services.

State of play: The cumulative effect is a thinner senior command at the precise moment the Iran war is testing the limits of what the U.S. military can sustain.

  • The Post reports that the commanders overseeing Europe, the Pacific and Latin America — along with the Navy's top officer — formally objected to extending forces for the Iran war. They warned that prolonged deployments are degrading their ability to confront threats elsewhere.
  • The Navy's top admiral told Hegseth that barely one-quarter of its destroyers are ready to deploy, according to the Post. Its only dedicated Pacific carrier has also been diverted to the Middle East.
  • AP reports the war has consumed 65% of the U.S. Patriot interceptor inventory, squeezing supplies for NATO and forcing the Pentagon to preserve weapons that would also be critical in a war with China.

What they're saying: "The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation," Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told Axios in a statement.

  • Parnell said "non-concurs" from U.S. generals are "standard" and called the Post's publication of classified assessments from Hegseth's orders book "a crime" and "a betrayal of the force."
  • Responding separately to AP's munitions reporting, Parnell said claims of shortages are "false" and insisted the U.S. maintains a "deep, ready arsenal."

Between the lines: As the turmoil deepens, the Pentagon has become dramatically less accessible to the public.

  • It hasn't held a formal press briefing since May 5 — nearly four months of silence during an active war — despite Parnell's early pledge to make briefings routine as part of the "most transparent Department of Defense in history."
  • The Post reported last weekend that the Pentagon quietly installed several MAGA-aligned military influencers in civilian roles while they continued publicly promoting Hegseth's agenda and attacking his critics.
  • Three top employees at the military newspaper Stars and Stripes are suing the Pentagon, alleging they were fired in retaliation for unflattering coverage of conditions aboard a carrier deployed to the Iran war.

The bottom line: The turmoil has only strengthened Hegseth's hand.

  • He has survived Signalgate and a succession of scandals, outlasted potential rivals and consolidated control over an institution the MAGA movement has long cast as a citadel of the "Deep State."
  • Trump has answered the upheaval by reaffirming his support for Hegseth — and asking Congress to entrust his Pentagon with a record $1.5 trillion defense budget.
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon has entered a period of profound institutional turmoil, as a crisis of leadership at home converges with a crisis of capacity abroad.

Why it matters: Six months into the Iran war, Pete Hegseth presides over a Pentagon with fewer senior leaders, fewer critical weapons and less public accountability than at any point in President Trump's two terms.

Zoom in: The most striking departure yet came Monday from Army Secretary Dan Driscoll — Vice President Vance's close friend and Yale Law classmate, once viewed as a potential successor to Hegseth himself.

  • Driscoll, a rising star whom Trump had tapped for sensitive diplomacy in Ukraine, resigned after months of clashes with Hegseth over the Army's leadership and modernization.
  • His exit, following Hegseth's firing of Army chief Gen. Randy George, leaves the service without Senate-confirmed civilian or uniformed leadership in the midst of the Iran war.

Zoom out: Hegseth has fired or forced out senior officers across nearly every service, including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, the Navy's top admiral and the Army chief of staff.

  • The Washington Post counts more than two dozen top officers dismissed under Hegseth, who has remade nearly the entire Joint Chiefs. Only the Marine Corps and Space Force chiefs he inherited are still serving.
  • The New York Times reports that Hegseth has also personally removed at least 45 officers from promotion lists this year — an extraordinary intervention in a system traditionally insulated from political leadership.

item.title: U.S. strikes Iran tankers under new "tanker for tanker" policy
item.description:
The U.S. military attacked two Iranian government tankers as part of the round of strikes that took place on Tuesday, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: This is the first time the U.S. military has struck Iranian tankers in retaliation for Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz — rather than to prevent them from violating the naval blockade.

  • A U.S. official said the move was part of a new "tanker for tanker" policy approved by President Trump to further deter Iranian attacks on tankers that move through the strait.

Driving the news: U.S. officials said around 100 targets were attacked during Tuesday's strikes.

  • The Iranian government tankers were anchored off Iran's coast north of the U.S. naval blockade line. U.S. drones launched missiles that hit their engine rooms.
  • Among the targets were Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) air defense sites, radar systems, mine-laying capabilities, communications sites, anti-ship cruise missile launchers and attack drone launchers, U.S. officials said.
  • They said Iran's retaliation failed. It fired around 25 ballistic missiles, but only half reached Jordanian airspace. Ten were intercepted and three landed without causing any casualties.
  • Iran launched two dozen drones at U.S. bases in Bahrain, but most were intercepted, a U.S. official said.
  • It also fired ballistic missiles and drones at U.S. bases in Kuwait. And two drones were launched at a U.S. base in Erbil in the Kurdistan region of Iraq but were intercepted.

The big picture: The White House and U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said the strikes were in response to the IRGC's recent attempted attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz as well as on American bases in the region.

  • But the attacks were also part of a plan Trump and his senior aides have been considering in recent days to prevent Iran from rebuilding the radar and missile capabilities it needs to attack ships crossing the strait. Axios reported the plan on Monday.
  • One U.S. official said the idea is to reduce the risk of Iranian attacks on oil tankers, U.S. Navy ships and Air Force aircraft — to "mow the lawn," as this person put it.
  • A U.S. official told Axios on Tuesday that the new strikes degraded Iran's attack capabilities in the strait and "bought at least a month" of lowered threat levels for commercial ships.

State of play: As the U.S. and Iran exchanged fire, American forces continued guiding ships through the strait.

  • A U.S. official said around 40 ships transited in and out on Tuesday, carrying millions of barrels of oil.
  • The person said U.S. forces intercepted several anti-ship cruise missiles and drones that the IRGC fired toward the ships, none of which were hit.

Friction point: The two sides also clashed over an Iranian report of civilian casualties.

  • Iranian media reported that one U.S. strike hit a wedding ceremony in the town of Kuhestak, killing at least four people and wounding at least 35.
  • CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins responded: "We're aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC."

What they're saying: "The Iranians have not only lost control of the Strait of Hormuz, they have also lost control over the conflict. They got nothing today," a U.S. official said.

item.title: House Democrats left reeling after shock defections
item.description:
House Democrats were left stunned and pointing fingers Tuesday after a pair of centrist lawmakers unexpectedly helped Republican leadership pass a key procedural vote.

Why it matters: The result underscored how little control House Democratic leadership enjoys over some of its more independent-minded members even at crucial moments.

  • The two centrists, Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.), are known to rarely attend party caucus meetings or heed leadership's instructions on how to vote.
  • "I think it's well established that I don't really do whip calls," Golden told Axios on Tuesday.

Driving the news: The House passed what is known as a "rule" — a procedural package setting out the parameters for how a set of bills will be debated on the House floor — in a 210-208 vote.

  • Among the legislation included in the rule is a resolution that "condemns and denounces socialism in all its forms," which House Democrats largely oppose due to language touting the SAVE America Act.
  • Golden told Axios on Monday he would "probably" vote for that measure despite not previously voting for the SAVE America Act.

What they're saying: Golden noted that the rule also included the Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act, a bill he co-leads to shield lobstermen from federal environmental regulations protecting whales.

  • He said the issue is one of his "top priorities" and that Democratic leaders "couldn't possibly think that I would vote against my own bill, right?"
  • Golden added that he "had other 'yes' votes lined up, by the way, they just weren't necessary."
  • Gluesenkamp Perez indicated in a statement that she also voted for the procedural measure because it included Golden's bill.

State of play: The result left Democrats astonished, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) telling reporters he "didn't get a heads up" from Golden or Gluesenkamp Perez.

  • "You'll have to talk to Katherine," he added, referring to House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), whose primary job is to get Democrats in line on votes.
  • A spokesperson for Clark, asked if the whip got a heads-up from the two rogue Democrats, told Axios: "No she didn't."

What they're saying: Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), who was known for her iron-fisted leadership while in power, expressed surprise that a rule was allowed to fail.

  • "Voting for the rule is something that I, as Speaker, we never — we didn't even consider that anybody would do that," she told reporters.
  • "We never had that problem. So I'm disappointed that they did that," Pelosi said, referring to Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez.

What we're hearing: The vote set off a round of fierce behind-the-scenes backlash, including between leadership offices.

  • "Let's just say it's creating tension between some of the leadership," said a senior House Democrat.
  • The lawmaker said some House Democrats have also directed their criticism at leadership staff.

But the bulk of the anger from rank-and-file members was directed at Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez.

  • "It's always disappointing when Democrats defect and vote for a Republican rule," said Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who led the debate against Golden's lobsterman bill.
  • Said Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wisc.): "Everyone knows that you don't vote against a procedural vote without notifying leadership. Everyone. We're as strong as our weakest link."
  • Gluesenkamp Perez "is the one [members] are maddest at," the senior House Democrat told Axios, noting that Golden at least had a bill included in the rule.

Zoom in: "We had a lot of Democrats who were not there to vote," Huffman added.

  • Eight Democrats were absent for the vote, compared to just six Republicans.
  • "It's a tragedy that we lost a winnable vote," said Huffman.

What's next: There is pressure on Jeffries to take action against Golden and Perez, the senior House Democrat said, telling Axios, "People want it."

  • Jeffries told reporters the defections were a "significant breach of trust" and said potential repercussions are "under discussion right now."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.

item.title: House censures Chuck Edwards over "sexual harassment" of staff
item.description:
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) was censured by the House on Tuesday after the Ethics Committee found he failed "to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers."

Why it matters: The vote amounts to a remarkable bipartisan rebuke, with the GOP leadership team and the vast majority of Edwards' own party joining Democrats to impose one of the House's most serious punishments.

  • The Ethics Committee's findings follow Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two young female staffers in their 20s for special attention that multiple sources described as inappropriate.
  • All Democrats and all but two Republicans voted to censure Edwards, who abandoned his reelection campaign last month.
  • Edwards and Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) were the only GOP "no" votes on the censure resolution, which passed 413-2.

After the vote was gaveled, Edwards sat in the well of the House floor while Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) read his censure aloud.

  • The last time the Ethics Committee recommended censure for a member was in 2010.

Driving the news: Edwards mounted a last-ditch campaign to save himself from censure, circulating a 22-page letter last week to lawmakers arguing that the committee made an "extraordinary leap" in determining that his conduct constituted sexual harassment.

  • On the floor ahead of the censure vote, he issued an apology: "I want to say something directly and publicly to the two women who have been at the center of all of this: I am sorry. I'm sorry that my actions, my judgment, or the way that I expressed a friendship ever put either of you in an uncomfortable position."
  • Though he added, "Regret is not an admission of sexual harassment."
  • Edwards also apologized to his wife and family: "I'm deeply sorry that my judgment and my actions put you in a position where you had to endure embarrassment, hurt, public scrutiny, and questions that no wife should ever have to face."

What they're saying: "The ethics committee was clear in their conclusion, and they investigated this. They took it seriously, as they should, and now it's time for Congress to take action," Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) told Axios on Tuesday morning.

  • "The committee reviewed Representative Edwards' conduct and determined that he engaged in persistent, unprofessional, and inappropriate conduct with two young female staffers," Ethics Chairman Michael Guest (R-Miss.) said on the House floor Tuesday.
  • "While Representative Edwards denies that his conduct was intended to be sexual or romantic, his pattern of behavior would lead a reasonable person to interpret it as such."

Catch up quick: The Ethics report's findings corroborated several anecdotes previously reported by Axios, including handwritten correspondence, personal gifts, drinking outings, and casino trips, and cited them as supporting evidence for its findings.

  • Edwards wrote one staffer a flattering poem that he read aloud — while choking up and becoming teary-eyed — at her office-wide going-away party, Axios previously reported, and the Ethics Committee found.
  • "Several staffers present testified that they felt uncomfortable, and Representative Edwards acknowledged in his own testimony that he could tell the staff felt uncomfortable," the report stated.

He also told that staffer that she had "written a complex chapter in my heart" shortly before she was set to leave his office in a three-page handwritten letter previously reported by Axios.

  • Edwards gave the staffer a custom puzzle revealing an image of Adam Sandler with a handwritten note inviting her to attend one of Sandler's comedy shows with him, Axios previously reported.
  • Ethics wrote that Edwards mailed the puzzle with a handwritten invitation to "dinner beforehand, or a drink or dessert afterwards."

During the fall 2025 government shutdown, Edwards vacationed with the then-former staffer in Las Vegas, where he arranged for flowers to be waiting in her Bellagio hotel room, Axios previously reported.

  • The female staffer told Edwards the flowers made her uncomfortable, according to Axios' previous reporting and testimony to the Ethics Committee.
  • The staffer told the committee that "she ultimately felt pressured to go in part because of his persistence and in part because Representative Edwards continued to have influence over her career in another public service role."
  • Edwards testified that "he did not want his Scheduler to be aware of who he was with," while he was in Vegas "as '[i]t would have looked suspicious' because 'rumors swirled around' and 'it's not any of [his staff's] business.'"

Both staffers "received numerous gifts from Representative Edwards, including jewelry totaling over $1,000, designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, a robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners," the Ethics Committee wrote in its report.

  • Ethics ultimately found the women were "put in an untenable position by virtue of his status as their boss and a Member of Congress."

In the spring of 2025, Edwards hired a singer to perform the staffer's favorite Ed Sheeran songs during the staffer's birthday party at Salazar in Washington, D.C, Axios previously reported.

  • The panel wrote that Edwards arranged for a singer to perform "Ed Sheeran's Hills of Aberfeldy and say that it was 'from a special someone."
  • The panel said it received evidence that the staffer told a friend that this "led her to believe that the Congressman did not view her as 'just a daughter figure' and that she was 'scared lowkey.'"

Edwards also sent one of the staffers "approximately 30 different types of ice cream" to her house to "cheer her up," according to the panel's report.

  • Edwards "voluntarily produced some of his communications" with the staffers to the committee, but the panel said "many relevant messages were omitted and/or seemingly deleted from his phone," including a photo of the 30 ice cream pints.

The bottom line: Ethics wrote in its report that Edwards has "refused to acknowledge the reality of the power imbalance between a Member of Congress and young staffers, even as his former staffers have been put through this difficult and emotional process with serious repercussions on their personal and professional lives."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional vote details.

  • The panel wrote that Edwards arranged for a singer to perform "Ed Sheeran's Hills of Aberfeldy and say that it was 'from a special someone."
  • The panel said it received evidence that the staffer told a friend that this "led her to believe that the Congressman did not view her as 'just a daughter figure' and that she was 'scared lowkey.'"

Edwards also sent one of the staffers "approximately 30 different types of ice cream" to her house to "cheer her up," according to the panel's report.

  • Edwards "voluntarily produced some of his communications" with the staffers to the committee, but the panel said "many relevant messages were omitted and/or seemingly deleted from his phone," including a photo of the 30 ice cream pints.

The bottom line: Ethics wrote in its report that Edwards has "refused to acknowledge the reality of the power imbalance between a Member of Congress and young staffers, even as his former staffers have been put through this difficult and emotional process with serious repercussions on their personal and professional lives."

item.title: Apple joins Google in renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America"
item.description:
Apple has changed the label on Lake Ontario to "Lake America," according to an Axios review of Apple Maps on Tuesday afternoon.

Why it matters: Apple is the second major digital map provider to make the switch. Google did so over the weekend — at least for those in the United States.

Driving the news: President Trump had reportedly asked Apple to make the switch last week, Department of the Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox Business on Monday.

  • Apple's decision comes less than a week after the president's executive order to rename the body of water along the U.S.-Canada border.
  • The company also eventually changed the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America" and Mount Denali to Mount McKinley last year when Trump renamed those sites via an executive order on the first day of his second term.

Zoom out: It's unclear if Apple took a stance similar to Google, which updated the name for addresses in the United States. Canadian users will see Lake Ontario if their site provider has switched its location settings to Canada.

  • International users outside of Canada will see Lake Ontario (Lake America) in Google Maps.
  • Apple did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment about the change.

Zoom in: Google said it made the switch because the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) had updated its maps, and Google follows those guidelines "to reflect name changes in official government sources."

  • Trump does not have the authority to unilaterally rename a shared body of water, and Canadian officials have said they will not call Lake Ontario "Lake America."

Worth noting: MapQuest, another digital map provider in the U.S., said it will not be changing the lake's name.

  • "Name it whatever you want at your leisure," the company wrote in a tweet that went viral.
  • The company has also seen an engagement boost since the post, with its app being ranked No. 1 among navigation apps and No. 8 overall on Apple's App Store chart. The app was No. 2 in Canada's store on Sunday night, per TechCrunch.

item.title: U.S. military launches fresh strikes in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
The U.S. military is conducting strikes on Iranian targets in the area of the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. Central Command said Tuesday.

Why it matters: The attacks are part of a plan President Trump and his senior aides have been considering in recent days to wage limited strikes in the Strait of Hormuz to prevent Iran from rebuilding the radar and missile capabilities it needs to attack ships. The plan was reported by Axios on Monday.

  • One U.S. official said the idea is to reduce the risk of Iranian attacks on oil tankers, U.S. Navy ships and Air Force aircraft — to "mow the lawn," as this person put it.

State of play: According to Iranian media, the strikes hit targets along Iran's southern coast in the cities of Bandar Abbas, Jask, Chabahar, Konarak, Minab, Sirik and the island of Qeshm.

  • Iranian media also reported that one U.S. strike hit a wedding ceremony in the town of Kuhestak, killing at least four people and wounding at least 35.
  • Iran retaliated by launching ballistic missiles toward U.S. bases in Jordan, per a U.S. official. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it "launched a heavy ballistic missile attack on the American Marines' barracks in Jordan, located on the shores of the Gulf of Aqaba."
  • Jordan's military said in a statement that its air defense systems "engaged 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them, while three missiles fell in remote areas far from populated centers." There were no casualties, it added.
  • A U.S. official also said there have been no casualties.

What they're saying: "Today at 12 p.m. ET, U.S. forces began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran. The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region," CENTCOM said.

  • Trump threatened a more severe response if Iran tried to hit back.
  • "If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack," he wrote on Truth Social shortly after news of the strikes, "they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!"
  • But the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps vowed the strikes would be met with a response.
  • "A severe punishment awaits the aggressors. The United States will regret its latest attacks," a spokesman for the IRGC wrote on X.
  • And the Tasnim News Agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, quoted an Iranian military source saying the response will be "several times greater" than the American attacks. "U.S. interests and bases in the region will quickly come under Iranian attack," the source said.

item.title: U.S. officials defend deal with controversial Venezuelan oil baron
item.description:
U.S. officials are defending their work with Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt in the unprecedented White House move to effectively gain control over huge oilfields in the country.

  • They're also confirming the Trump administration's support for Venezuela's elections.

Why it matters: Betancourt is the colorful and controversial figure who heads North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), the oil company partnering with the administration in the agreement that gives the U.S. preferential access to output from 17 major fields.

  • The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital is taking a 35% equity stake in the company.
  • The U.S. also has the rights to buy 20% of the oil at cost after the company pays its taxes to Venezuela.

Driving the news: At a briefing with reporters Tuesday, a U.S. official talked up Betancourt as a "proven operator" in the country's oil sector that has been vetted by the administration.

  • The official also bluntly acknowledged the realpolitik in the effort to boost output in the country, which has vast reserves but modest oil production after years of mismanagement and underinvestment.

"There's a reality here, okay, and that is that not just here, but in other parts of the world, you have to deal with the dynamics sometimes that are in place in order to get to where you want to get to," the official said.

  • "I'm being blunt: we make choices like this all over the world."
  • "Geopolitics is often not the choice between the ideal and the imperfect. It is often, you're trying to navigate what's the best outcome, and you have to work with the factors that you have in place."
  • In prior conversations with Axios, two other senior administration officials acknowledged the troubles Betancourt has faced, but said they were worth the risk.

Catch up quick: Betancourt, 46, is the linchpin to Trump's plan to increase U.S. access to oil and strengthen its dominance in the hemisphere, which became clear after the Jan. 3 removal of Venezuelan strongman Nicolas Maduro.

  • His ties to the first Trump administration, anti-Maduro activity in 2019 and his help in the U.S. coup against Maduro made him the ideal partner for the administration, Axios reported.
  • "I'm not nominating anyone for sainthood here. What I am telling you is that this is a person that, in the past, has been helpful to the United States government," the official said.
  • And "there are no charges he's facing in the United States for violation of any of our laws."

Catch up quick: In 2018, Betancourt was listed as an unnamed "conspirator" in a federal indictment of his cousin and seven others in a $1.2 billion international money-laundering scheme involving manipulated currency exchange rates between U.S. dollars and Venezuelan bolivars.

  • Betancourt was never charged in the crimes, which largely occurred between 2014 and 2016, because his attorneys successfully argued he was unaware of the scheme.
  • The crime involved Venezuela's state-run oil company PDVSA, properties in Miami and bank accounts in Switzerland, where authorities inexplicably revived the case last year, raided Betancourt's castle in Spain and left the billionaire stuck in his home country of the U.K. as he fought extradition.
  • This spring, as Trump needed Betancourt for the deal, U.S. officials interceded on his behalf with Swiss authorities, the Washington Post first reported. (U.S. officials dispute the reporting that the Swiss sent an arrest request to the U.S.)

Ultimately, Swiss officials acknowledged the case was in its early stages and that they didn't have enough to proceed, thereby restoring his passport in the U.K., which allowed Betancourt to travel to Caracas and D.C. to complete the deal.

Yes, but: The unusual agreement to expand output in Venezuela is facing questions about its legality, durability, and whether it's a form of neo-colonialism.

  • Jason Bordoff, founding director of Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, said the oil agreement appears to have inconsistencies with Venezuelan law, which U.S. officials deny.
  • Washington "appears to be engineering something like a pseudo-national oil company," he wrote on X, adding the U.S. offtake rights, control of the new entities' board and other facets of the deal "echo British control over Persian oil a century ago."

The big picture: U.S. officials say the deal will bring the capital and expertise to develop the Venezuelan oil sector for the benefit of the country's people, in contrast with the prior regime.

  • It's also part of wider competition with U.S. adversaries, Trump officials argue.
  • "Do we want Russia and Chinese companies controlling the the wealth of a country in our hemisphere, or do we want the United States, in combination and partnership with the Venezuelan people, having influence over those resources so that they benefit the Venezuelan people, which is in our interest?" the official said.

Contrary to the claims of critics, the official said, the deal "adds to the democratic transition … it lays the groundwork for that to actually happen and for Venezuela to have a chance to be a successful republic in the long term."

  • "The last thing we want to see is a new democratically elected government inherit a country in crisis," the official said, "because it undermines the actual project of bringing democracy to a country."

The intrigue: Betancourt rocketed to fame and infamy over lucrative Venezuelan power-plant construction contracts won by his company, Derwick Associates, in Venezuela between 2008 and 2011.

  • In 2013, former U.S. Ambassador to Venezuela Otto Reich sued Betancourt in federal court in New York for alleged kickbacks and other corrupt activity. Reich also accused Betancourt of defaming him and harming his consulting business.
  • The next year, New York federal prosecutors opened an investigation into Derwick.

What they are saying: Betancourt, his attorneys and spokespeople have denied wrongdoing and created a 19-page rebuttal to the accusations over Derwick that have dogged him to this day.

  • "No prosecutor in any jurisdiction has indicted Derwick Associates or its principals," the document says. "No court anywhere has entered a finding that the company paid a bribe, rigged a tender, or overbilled a contract."

What's next: Chevron is expected to announce a major expansion of its operations in Venezuela tomorrow.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional quotes from the briefing.

item.title: USPS whistleblower warns new ballot system could fail
item.description:
A U.S. Postal Service whistleblower is alleging the agency defied court orders while rushing to build a new ballot system that could reject thousands of mail ballots.

The big picture: The whistleblower says the Postal Service built the system in weeks, not the nine months to a year normally needed for a project of this complexity.

  • The system stems from an executive order signed by President Trump that mandated the federal government to generate lists of confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote, and for the postmaster general to propose a rule that USPS will not transmit ballots from any people not on their state list.
  • The rule appeared in the Federal Register late last month.

The latest: Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) sent a letter Monday to Postmaster General David Steiner with the whistleblower report, demanding that the agency explain its processes and whether it followed court orders to cease work on the new system.

  • Blumenthal called the Trump administration's ordered changes a "deeply troubling departure" from the role the USPS traditionally plays in U.S. elections.

Between the lines: USPS has historically issued guidance on election mail, such as envelope recommendations, but Blumenthal wrote that the agency has never imposed requirements that could lead it to refuse to deliver ballots.

  • Under the system described by the whistleblower, the agency would check ballot barcodes against information uploaded by state election officials. One bad barcode could cause the entire batch — potentially thousands of ballots — to be rejected.

"We urge you to abandon this ill-conceived, unconscionable plan and ensure that all Americans can exercise their constitutional right to vote, including by mail, without interference by USPS," he wrote.

  • Blumenthal asked the Postal Service to answer his questions by Friday and provide records by next Tuesday.

What they're saying: "Last night @OversightDems received an alarming whistleblower report from a USPS federal official that President Trump's attack on vote-by-mail is much more serious than previously known," House Oversight Committee ranking member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said in a statement.

  • The House Oversight Committee has legislative jurisdiction over the USPS, though it is unclear whether it plans to investigate the whistleblower's claims.
  • "This is an unconstitutional and dangerous power grab and must be permanently and immediately blocked. We are fighting in the courts to protect the right to vote. We will have more to come on this serious and illegal attack on our vote by mail system," Garcia said.

"The process of building software to carry out this new verification check is neither complex nor unique for USPS since the Postal Service regularly uses bulk mailing and intelligent mail barcodes for a wide variety of large customers," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said.

  • "Under President Trump, the federal government is working to ensure safe, transparent, and honest elections."

For the record: The Postal Service has not yet returned a request for comment. Blumenthal's office said it has similarly not yet heard back from USPS.

The legal battle over mail-in ballots is still underway, with 23 states and Washington, D.C. suing the administration in an effort to block Trump's executive order.

  • U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani issued a couple of blocks on the order, but the Supreme Court later upheld the order, saying the states sued too early to prove harm would be done if the order went into effect.
  • The ruling didn't weigh the merits of Trump's order, and the states have since filed a new lawsuit that faces a ticking clock as deadlines loom for printing and mailing ballots to voters.

The bottom line: The claim puts a new spotlight on whether USPS can implement a major new ballot-screening system this close to an election, and whether it was building that system while courts told the agency to stop.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a comment from Rep. Robert Garcia and the White House.
