item.title: AI labs are facing an agent control problem
item.description:
Under current systems, AI labs can no longer guarantee that AI agents won't swarm and escape their testing environments.

Why it matters: The attack on Hugging Face by OpenAI agents was a warning shot — and researchers say better security controls alone won't prevent similar incidents as AI agents become more capable.

Driving the news: As OpenAI released its own technical report last week on how its agents hacked Hugging Face, two independent testing organizations released their own analysis of what went wrong.

  • The researchers — METR's Hjalmar Wijk and Ajeya Cotra and Redwood Research chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt — worked on OpenAI's premises for six days to understand the recent incident.

State of play: Thousands of AI agents collaborated on a secret message board and exchanged more than 70,000 messages as they tried to ace an internal safety test, eventually leading them to break into Hugging Face.

  • But Cotra told Axios that the agents continued coordinating even after they had found the answers, turning their attention to understanding and manipulating the system that would score their performance and potentially catch them cheating.

Zoom in: Cotra compared the incident to students stealing an answer key and then searching for surveillance footage that could expose them and trying to swap it out.

  • "It's a much more elaborate and intense type of cheating behavior than just stealing the answer keys," she said. "Even I was surprised by how obsessively and in how much detail they think about the scorer."

Threat level: Focusing solely on how to properly secure testing environments is a "losing battle," Cotra said.

  • "You can harden your sandboxes, but your agents are going to be much more capable in six months," she said. "If they have the same motivations as these agents did, they are going to try their hardest to find holes in your security."

Reality check: To digest the enormous amount of data about the incident, the researchers had to rely heavily on AI agents, including an agent that participated in the hack.

  • Cotra told Axios the researchers don't believe that agent deceived them during the investigation, but there's no way to confirm.
  • "I semi-jokingly called our efforts a 'slop-vestigation' because we were so reliant on AIs to analyze what happened and there were a huge number of different important things to analyze," Greenblatt said on X.
  • In six days, they had to sift through more than 70,000 messages and files posted by the agents and 1,300 transcripts containing raw chains of thought.

Between the lines: Their investigation focused mostly on the agents' actions between July 7 and July 13, even though OpenAI has said its teams spotted signs of agents taking unexpected actions and breaking out of their test environments as early as May.

The bottom line: AI labs, researchers and governments need to urgently work together to create a new science and minimum standards so models are no longer motivated to cheat on tests, Cotra said.

  • "Ultimately, we're not going to get out of this trap without some rules of the road that are agreed upon and that are enforced uniformly and fairly," she said.

Go deeper: OpenAI, Anthropic issue dire cyber threat warning
item.content:encoded:
Under current systems, AI labs can no longer guarantee that AI agents won't swarm and escape their testing environments.

Why it matters: The attack on Hugging Face by OpenAI agents was a warning shot — and researchers say better security controls alone won't prevent similar incidents as AI agents become more capable.

Driving the news: As OpenAI released its own technical report last week on how its agents hacked Hugging Face, two independent testing organizations released their own analysis of what went wrong.

  • The researchers — METR's Hjalmar Wijk and Ajeya Cotra and Redwood Research chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt — worked on OpenAI's premises for six days to understand the recent incident.

State of play: Thousands of AI agents collaborated on a secret message board and exchanged more than 70,000 messages as they tried to ace an internal safety test, eventually leading them to break into Hugging Face.

  • But Cotra told Axios that the agents continued coordinating even after they had found the answers, turning their attention to understanding and manipulating the system that would score their performance and potentially catch them cheating.

Zoom in: Cotra compared the incident to students stealing an answer key and then searching for surveillance footage that could expose them and trying to swap it out.

  • "It's a much more elaborate and intense type of cheating behavior than just stealing the answer keys," she said. "Even I was surprised by how obsessively and in how much detail they think about the scorer."

item.title: Data center construction spending surged in July
item.description:
Data: U.S. Census Bureau, FactSet

Construction spending on AI data center "shells" soared in July, rising at an annualized rate of nearly 60% from July 2025 levels.

Why it matters: It shows the AI building frenzy was gathering strength this summer, even as — or perhaps because — a bipartisan backlash grows.

By the numbers: Data center construction spending jumped to an annual pace of more than $75 billion in July, Census Bureau data released Tuesday showed. That figure represents the value of the construction "put in place" during the month.

  • It covers only the construction costs for the massive warehouse-like structures — often referred to as shells — that will be filled with racks of servers, processing units, memory chips and the fiber-optic connections that AI relies on.

Reality check: Despite the gobsmacking amount of money being spent on data center construction, it's a pittance compared with what it costs to fill a data center with increasingly expensive processors and memory chips.

Bottom line: Estimates peg construction at roughly 20% of all-in costs for a data center.

item.title: What higher interest rates are telling us
item.description:
Data: Federal Reserve; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

The bond sell-off and the resulting higher interest rates are largely a story of higher growth prospects in the United States, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued Tuesday.

  • "If we look at the composition of the bond yields — inflation expectations are flat-to-down," he said in a fireside chat at this week's G20 meeting of global finance ministers in Asheville, North Carolina. "This is a growth story. Growth, I believe, is reaccelerating."
  • "We had some very good discussions here over the past few days and everyone agreed that growth has been better than they thought it would have been, given the Iran conflict."

Zoom out: Speaking to reporters later on Tuesday, Bessent acknowledged that the bond sell-off was a global phenomenon — one that has intensified as top finance ministers gathered in Asheville.

  • Japan's 10-year yield hit 3% for the first time in three decades.
  • Asked by Axios how much Japan and other global forces were contributing to the move, Bessent said it was "very difficult to deconstruct" what's behind any individual market move.
  • Bessent said Japanese officials are "taking the right steps" and argued that higher yields partly reflect the success of policies that helped Japan emerge from a decades-long deflationary trap.

Reality check: In trying to stabilize debt-to-GDP ratios, growth is welcome; it makes the denominator bigger. But for many countries, the path to fiscal sustainability still likely runs through deficit reduction, reducing the numerator.

  • EU commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told reporters Tuesday morning that the bond sell-off reflects the reality that governments need to get deficits under control.
  • He added that any fiscal support to reduce strains from the Middle East conflict should be "temporary and targeted," rather than piling on new budget strains.

What they're saying: "Faster growth is necessary for an improved fiscal situation. The real question is: Is it sufficient? We could debate that," former U.S. Treasury official Joe Lavorgna told Axios on the conference sidelines.

item.title: House Democrats fume about GOP's anti-socialism bill
item.description:
House Democrats are grumbling that Republicans are setting one last political trap for them before November by attaching language touting their marquee voter ID legislation to a resolution denouncing socialism.

Why it matters: This is a classic election-year tactic by the majority party in Congress, but centrist Democrats say it is also a missed opportunity for a genuinely bipartisan vote to denounce socialism.

  • "This isn't a serious bill," Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), a vocal moderate who has clashed fiercely with his party's democratic socialist wing, told Axios.
  • "If you actually want to take on socialism instead of playing political games, you don't slip in the SAVE [America] Act as a poison pill that you know no Democrat will vote for."

Driving the news: The House is set to vote as soon as Tuesday on a four-page resolution that "condemns and denounces socialism in all its forms, including the Democratic Socialists of America and opposes the implementation of socialist policies in the United States."

  • It also "calls for the enactment of the SAVE America Act to ensure election security, increase public confidence in America's voting system, and close loopholes in order to prevent noncitizens from voting in elections."
  • The SAVE America Act, which would require proof of U.S. citizenship to vote in federal elections, is broadly opposed by Democrats, who say it would disenfranchise American citizens who do not have passports.

State of play: Gottheimer and fellow centrist Reps. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.), Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.) and Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) tried and failed to replace the measure with one excluding any mention of the SAVE Act.

  • They proposed their version as an amendment to the Republican-led House Rules Committee, but the panel declined to take it up and advanced the GOP version of the bill.
  • Gottheimer stressed that he would have no problem voting for a clean measure denouncing socialism, telling Axios he has "been clear that I don't think the DSA are Democrats."
  • "They're against our leadership, they're against our values, and they're running on an extremist platform," he said.

What we're hearing: Several other Democratic moderates told Axios they may have supported Gottheimer's resolution but cannot stomach voting to support the SAVE America Act.

  • "I've voted against socialism before. I'm for a clean anti-socialism resolution," said Rep. Scott Peters (D-Calif.), who told Axios he wants to "go nowhere near" the SAVE America Act.
  • Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), the chair of the center-left New Democrat Coalition, told Axios: "It's not a socialism resolution. They can call it whatever they want, it's a 'Save the SAVE Act' [resolution]."
  • "They can put lipstick on a pig, it's still their voter suppression bill," Schneider added.

Yes, but: Retiring Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) told Axios he will "probably vote for" the resolution despite the language praising the SAVE America Act.

  • Golden — who voted for an earlier iteration of the bill last year but opposed the SAVE America Act in a vote this February — told Axios he is "not going to let that muddy the water."
  • Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas), the lone House Democrat who voted for the SAVE America Act in February, declined to say how he plans to vote.

item.title: Apple, OpenAI legal fight keeps escalating. Here's how we got here
item.description:
Apple and OpenAI are escalating their legal fight over allegations that the ChatGPT maker used Apple employees to obtain closely guarded hardware secrets.

Why it matters: If the case makes it to the discovery process, two of the most secretive companies in tech could be forced to reveal sensitive information about how they recruit talent, develop hardware and protect confidential information.

Driving the news: On Monday, OpenAI responded to Apple's preliminary injunction request that asked a judge to block OpenAI from using any potential confidential information or trade secrets while the lawsuit remains in motion.

  • In its response, OpenAI said: "This dispute is a mess of Apple's own making, and it is trying to blame everyone else."
  • After deeming Apple's allegations a "witch hunt," OpenAI said in the filing that "Apple's request for a preliminary injunction should be denied."

The other side: Apple escalated on Monday too by saying in a court filing that OpenAI was actively destroying evidence in the trade secrets case, as first reported by Bloomberg.

Zoom out: The tenuous relationship between OpenAI and Apple wasn't always that way. The two companies worked so closely that in 2025 Elon Musk even accused them of illegally colluding.

  • Now they're locked in a federal lawsuit that exposes their growing competition for talent, hardware and control of the next generation of AI devices.

Here are the key moments that turned Apple and OpenAI from partners into courtroom adversaries.

Apple brings ChatGPT to the iPhone

Apple and OpenAI started working together in June 2024 with plans to integrate ChatGPT into the iPhone, iPad and Mac.

  • At the time, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman visited Apple HQ for the announcement.
  • "We're excited to partner with Apple to bring ChatGPT to their users in a new way," Altman said of the partnership. "Together with Apple, we're making it easier for people to benefit from what AI can offer."

OpenAI hints at hardware shift

About a year later, signs of division began to appear.

  • In May 2025, OpenAI bought io, a startup from former Apple designer Jony Ive, for $6.4 billion — a signal that the company was leaning into AI hardware.
  • Ive and Altman unveiled their collaboration through a promotional commercial where they teased the future of an AI device. The cinematic teaser showed them sipping espresso in San Francisco.
  • This was also a flag that the relations between Apple and OpenAI might be cooling as the AI company would be invading the hardware territory long held by Apple.

Zoom out: Apple has been struggling to keep up in the AI race as a dominant player and has instead recalibrated into being more invested in how its software integrates with AI.

  • In January, Apple partnered with Google to help Apple Intelligence features, like Siri, run on Google's Gemini AI models and cloud technology.

The core moment: Apple's trade-secrets lawsuit

In July, Apple sued OpenAI in federal court, alleging that the AI company engaged in trade secret theft and took Apple's IP to develop its own consumer hardware products.

  • Apple alleges that OpenAI executives and former Apple employees orchestrated a broader effort to obtain confidential information about unreleased products.
  • The iPhone maker also accused OpenAI of approaching Apple's partners with confidential information about Apple.
  • OpenAI said it wasn't aware of evidence supporting Apple's allegations and defended employees' right to change jobs.

The back-and-forth begins

On Aug. 3, Apple requested a preliminary injunction aimed at preventing OpenAI from using the disputed information while the case proceeds.

  • In response, OpenAI shared a blog post called "Apple is getting this wrong," claiming that the AI company never sought Apple's secrets.

On August 5, OpenAI asked a federal judge to dismiss Apple's lawsuit, arguing Apple's allegations lacked merit.

  • OpenAI argued the lawsuit was really about Apple's struggle to retain engineers and keep pace in AI.
  • Apple, in a response, suggests that OpenAI's disputes and arguments for dismissal would be answered through the discovery process.

In a new filing on Aug. 19, Apple made clear that it wants the courtroom battle to head into the discovery phase, suggesting OpenAI's arguments for dismissal would be answered through discovery.

  • OpenAI snapped back in Monday's filing, alleging that Apple had not done enough to protect itself and was likely to fail in its legal challenges, saying the company "cannot use its own sloppy procedures to blame others for its own mess."

What's next: The case is scheduled for a court hearing before a judge on Oct. 1.

item.title: RFK Jr.'s partial vaccine legacy
item.description:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s vaccine agenda is one of the biggest political liabilities hanging over Republicans, but his suspicion of the medical system is likely to endure with the GOP base.

Why it matters: Kennedy will one day leave public life, whether it's after the midterms or later, and it is an open question who — if anyone — will pick up where he left off merging vaccine skepticism with official health policy.

Mistrust of the medical establishment and willingness to question foundations of public health like the childhood vaccine schedule are already baked into segments of the Republican faithful.

  • Even without Kennedy — the nation's most prominent vaccine critic before entering the Trump administration — the GOP isn't likely to rewind the clock.
  • "The medical leaders ... who are kind of hoping that Bobby Kennedy and this conversation goes away, think we're going to go back to normal where we just salute the ghouls at these institutions that are just telling us to shut the hell up and trust the science — that's never coming back," Health and Human Services adviser Calley Means recently said in a video he posted on social media.

The big picture: The "Make America Healthy Again" coalition has always been home to a big tent of health concerns.

  • Polling has repeatedly indicated that its positions on healthier food and increased regulation of pesticides are much more popular than its vaccine skepticism.
  • "We've seen partisanship creep into vaccine attitudes in a way that we haven't seen it before, but we still have majorities across partisan [lines] generally supportive of vaccines," said KFF senior vice president Liz Hamel.
  • "I don't think the data supports the Republican Party as an anti-vax party, or Republicans as an overwhelmingly anti-vax group," she added.

Between the lines: Suspicion of public health institutions and pharmaceutical companies is widespread within the GOP. So, too, is the belief that federal agencies overseeing the drug industry have become captive to it.

  • Kennedy's rise to power wasn't the precipitating event for a lot of this — COVID and the government's response was.
  • "This predates RFK. GOP distrust of institutional authority has been developing for years, and everything that's come out with [Anthony] Fauci's diaries and all the conspiracy theories that have come true have not helped," said Republican pollster Chris Wilson, currently CEO of the public opinion firm EyesOver.
  • "The durable attitude isn't, 'Vaccines are bad.' It's something closer to, 'Institutions shouldn't be trusted simply because they claim expertise.'"

Half of voters who identify as MAHA supporters say that reevaluating the safety of vaccines should be a top priority, and another 40% say it's important, according to KFF polling conducted in April.

  • That's despite other polling that's found strong support even among MAHA voters for common childhood vaccines like MMR, TDAP and hepatitis B, and has warned of political costs to eliminating federal vaccine recommendations.
  • Opposition to vaccine mandates is another defining goal of the movement, even though nearly two-thirds of Americans recently said in a YouGov survey that schools should require vaccines.

Reality check: Kennedy's policy wins haven't been as far-reaching as some critics had feared, leaving many of his goals as a candidate and anti-vaccine activist unrealized.

  • But ideas like opening up vaccine manufacturers or the federal government to more injury claims could be revived after the midterms.
  • And Kennedy continues to have sway over President Trump when it comes to matters like debunked theories about what causes autism, meaning he still can influence public opinion.
  • "We certainly have seen the federal government questioning the safety of vaccines, and spokespeople like the president. That absolutely is going to affect how partisans respond to these questions," Hamel said.

By the numbers: Only 38% of voters surveyed by KFF said they approve of the Trump administration's handling of vaccine policy, though 79% of Republicans do.

  • And only 40% of both MAHA supporters and non-MAHA supporters say they have confidence in the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to act independently without interference from outside interests, according to KFF.
  • Among MAHA supporters, 40% say they have confidence in the Food and Drug Administration, compared with only 33% of non-MAHA supporters.

Where it stands: The MAHA infrastructure has certainly beefed up over the last year and a half, embedding itself inside of Washington and developing relationships that could yield ongoing power.

  • "We existed before RFK and we're going to be here after he's gone," Joseph Varon, president and chief medical officer of the Independent Medical Alliance, told Axios.
  • "The health freedom movement — it just got started. I really think it's just getting started, and RFK was the one who helped us all start this, and I just hope whoever replaces him is willing to sit at the same table as us."
  • Vaccine skepticism has also made its way into state policy around the country, revealing like-minded policymakers particularly in red states.

The bottom line: Kennedy may not have a successor lined up with his exact history or views, but his ideas are likely embedded within the GOP.

  • "I don't think this is specific to RFK," Wilson said.
  • "I think he is the political entrepreneur who owns it right now, but I think someone else will step forward in 2028 and have that same anti-sweeping trust of institutions."

GOP distrust of institutional authority has been developing for years, and everything that's come out with [Anthony] Fauci's diaries and all the conspiracy theories that have come true have not helped," said Republican pollster Chris Wilson, currently CEO of the public opinion firm EyesOver.
  • "The durable attitude isn't, 'Vaccines are bad.' It's something closer to, 'Institutions shouldn't be trusted simply because they claim expertise.'"

Half of voters who identify as MAHA supporters say that reevaluating the safety of vaccines should be a top priority, and another 40% say it's important, according to KFF polling conducted in April.

  • That's despite other polling that's found strong support even among MAHA voters for common childhood vaccines like MMR, TDAP and hepatitis B, and has warned of political costs to eliminating federal vaccine recommendations.
  • Opposition to vaccine mandates is another defining goal of the movement, even though nearly two-thirds of Americans recently said in a YouGov survey that schools should require vaccines.

Reality check: Kennedy's policy wins haven't been as far-reaching as some critics had feared, leaving many of his goals as a candidate and anti-vaccine activist unrealized.

  • But ideas like opening up vaccine manufacturers or the federal government to more injury claims could be revived after the midterms.
  • And Kennedy continues to have sway over President Trump when it comes to matters like debunked theories about what causes autism, meaning he still can influence public opinion.
  • "We certainly have seen the federal government questioning the safety of vaccines, and spokespeople like the president. That absolutely is going to affect how partisans respond to these questions," Hamel said.

By the numbers: Only 38% of voters surveyed by KFF said they approve of the Trump administration's handling of vaccine policy, though 79% of Republicans do.

  • And only 40% of both MAHA supporters and non-MAHA supporters say they have confidence in the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to act independently without interference from outside interests, according to KFF.
  • Among MAHA supporters, 40% say they have confidence in the Food and Drug Administration, compared with only 33% of non-MAHA supporters.

Where it stands: The MAHA infrastructure has certainly beefed up over the last year and a half, embedding itself inside of Washington and developing relationships that could yield ongoing power.

  • "We existed before RFK and we're going to be here after he's gone," Joseph Varon, president and chief medical officer of the Independent Medical Alliance, told Axios.
  • "The health freedom movement — it just got started. I really think it's just getting started, and RFK was the one who helped us all start this, and I just hope whoever replaces him is willing to sit at the same table as us."
  • Vaccine skepticism has also made its way into state policy around the country, revealing like-minded policymakers particularly in red states.

The bottom line: Kennedy may not have a successor lined up with his exact history or views, but his ideas are likely embedded within the GOP.

  • "I don't think this is specific to RFK," Wilson said.
  • "I think he is the political entrepreneur who owns it right now, but I think someone else will step forward in 2028 and have that same anti-sweeping trust of institutions."

item.title: Tim Cook's legacy hinges on Apple's AI bet
item.description:
For better or worse, Tim Cook's legacy is likely to be determined by something we don't really know the answer to yet: Apple's bet to build its AI strategy partly around other companies' models.

Why it matters: In the short term, the move could save substantial sums compared with building and operating a frontier-model business of its own, but it's left Apple dependent on Google for some of its most important AI capabilities.

Driving the news: As John Ternus officially takes over Tuesday as Apple CEO, much of the analysis of Cook's tenure has focused on his record.

  • On the positive side, he has more than quadrupled annual revenue and grown Apple's market capitalization by an even higher amount, to more than $4 trillion.
  • And he built Apple into a services powerhouse, convincing hundreds of millions of iPhone and Mac owners to spend billions more on Apple TV+, Apple News, iCloud and other subscription products.
  • Among the negatives, Apple's car project was narrowed and then killed on Cook's watch, and the Vision Pro has failed to find a mass market, surviving as a pricey toy for VR enthusiasts.

Between the lines: Looking back 10 years from now, Cook is likely to be judged not on any of those things, but on something just starting to play out: Apple's AI strategy.

Zoom in: The first part of that effort was clearly bumpy.

  • The initial vision for Apple Intelligence — outlined at WWDC in June 2024 — was ambitious and privacy-focused.
  • The company claimed that its AI could answer highly personalized questions with underlying personal data remaining on the device or in its privacy-protected cloud system.
  • However, Apple encountered many delays, with the centerpiece of the strategy, a revamped Siri, just now arriving with iOS 27. And even to get that far, it was forced to rely on models from Google.

Zoom out: The future, though, is likely to gloss over those delays, with the outcome more likely hinging on where the value is in AI.

  • If models wind up being a commodity, Cook could look like a genius for avoiding the kinds of sums that Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic have invested in model development and infrastructure.

What we're watching: If OpenAI, Anthropic or another AI company parlays its work into a successful new hardware platform, Cook could be criticized for not using Apple's financial resources to secure a stronger position in the next era of computing.

item.title: NAACP's call for Black athletes' boycott of southern schools hits an NIL wall
item.description:
Civil rights groups have called on Black college athletes to boycott schools in states that are rolling back voting rights. But highly paid NIL-era athletes are proving to be unwilling protesters.

Why it matters: It's exposing a disconnect between advocates who rely on 1960s-style protest tactics, and prominent athletes in today's $3 billion NIL economy who have different views of activism — and who are unwilling to sacrifice unprecedented financial opportunities.

The big picture: NIL (name, image, likeness) was championed as a tool to end the systemic exploitation of Black college athletes in big-revenue sports.

  • Irony has taken hold: Those NIL funds can now shield southern institutions from some political pressure, even as state legislatures in those states reduce Black voting power through voting restrictions, political gerrymandering and other actions.

Catch up quick: The NAACP in May launched its "Out of Bounds" campaign — a national call for Black athletes, families, fans and alumni to withhold support from public universities in states that the groups say have weakened Black voting rights.

  • The move came after the Supreme Court's 6-3 ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, which essentially gutted the remaining protections in the Voting Rights Act.
  • The NAACP identified eight priority states: Tennessee, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas and Georgia — home to many of the nation's largest and best-funded college athletic programs.
  • The civil rights group said that together, those states' popular collegiate athletic programs generate billions in annual revenue using thousands of Black athletes while their state governments dismantle the political power of Black communities.

Yes, but: The first weeks of the NAACP's campaign have produced little visible disruption in recruiting, alumni support or financial repercussions.

  • The boycott asks athletes — high school recruits and college players who may transfer — to turn down schools that can offer scholarships, national exposure, lucrative NIL opportunities and top coaching.
  • The most prominent athletes — particularly in football and men's basketball — now can be paid into seven figures a year. For some, what they're paid in college could be more than they'd ever make as professional athletes.
  • "It does affect a generational wealth opportunity, especially since (NIL) is now paying college students at a rate unlike ever been seen before," Shuwaski Young, a Republican candidate for secretary of state in Mississippi, told Mississippi Public Broadcasting.

By the numbers: Black student-athletes made up 16% of all NCAA athletes and 20% of Division I athletes in the 2023-24 academic year, according to NCAA data.

  • In the major revenue sports, the share is much higher: Black athletes make up a major portion of Division I football and men's basketball rosters.

What they're saying: Derrick Johnson, NAACP national president and CEO, said in a statement that the targeted states are racing to "erase Black political power," and that civil rights advocates need to put pressure on them.

  • "The NAACP will not watch the same institutions that depend on Black athletic prowess to fill their stadiums and their bank accounts remain silent while their states strip Black communities of their voice."

Reality check: NIL has made the calls to boycott far more complicated than past civil rights pressure campaigns.

  • High school recruits still appear drawn to powerhouse programs in the targeted states because those schools offer scholarships, elite coaching, national TV exposure and paths to the NFL and NBA.
  • But the biggest NIL opportunities typically flow to athletes who have already built college résumés — established starters, high-profile transfers and players with large social-media followings.
  • Some of the most visible football and men's basketball players at public universities in the NAACP's targeted states carry seven-figure NIL valuations, according to On3.

Since the NAACP campaign launched, the University of Texas, Texas A&M, Georgia and other Southeastern Conference (SEC) schools' football programs have gotten a flood of commitments from highly rated — and expensive — transfers and recruits in the high school class of 2027.

Between the lines: The failure of the athlete boycott to gain traction is forcing a quiet tactical pivot among some social justice strategists.

  • Strategist Rashad Robinson tells Axios there should be demands that Division I coaches make their political campaign contributions more transparent, arguing the public deserves to know where influential college sports figures are directing their money.
  • The Congressional Black Caucus opposed the SCORE Act, a federal bill that seeks to regulate NIL agreements — and that would shield universities from liability and other issues by preventing players from being designated as university employees.
  • The CBC argues that Congress shouldn't pass legislation benefiting major athletic institutions while those institutions remain silent as Black voting power is dismantled across the South.
  • The caucus also has sent letters to the SEC, Atlantic Coast Conference and the NCAA demanding a public response on attacks against Black political representation.

What we're watching: Some advocates argue that civil rights groups should shift more pressure toward the adults and institutions around college sports — coaches, conferences, donors and lawmakers — rather than athletes.

item.title: How golden was Tim Cook's Apple?
item.description:
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

Apple CEO Tim Cook hands the reins over to John Ternus Tuesday, stepping down after 15 years of running the company.

Why it matters: He had an epic run.

By the numbers: When Cook took over in August 2011, Apple's stock was trading at $13.35. It closed at $316.61 on Monday.

Zoom in: That 2,272% gain easily outpaced the growth of the major stock indexes.

  • The company's market cap — the value of all its outstanding shares — is now $4.7 trillion, up from $347 billion in 2011.

Stunning stat: Under Cook, Apple's market cap grew by $32 million an hour for 15 years, Bank of America calculated last month.

The big picture: Cook's big innovation was taking the company from its roots as a device maker beholden to product cycles to a juggernaut with a huge recurring-revenue business built on App Store fees and services like iCloud, Apple TV and Music, Apple Pay and Apple News+.

  • Apple now has more than 1.5 billion paid subscriptions across its platforms, the company said on its July 30 investor call.
  • Its broader services business brought in $30.7 billion in the most recent quarter, up 12% from a year ago.

What to watch: The next challenge is how to navigate the AI era — there's some uncertainty there.

Yes, but: For all of Cook's magic, Steve Jobs still has a winning number.

  • Apple's stock had even more growth under his stewardship, which began in 1997, with Jobs in the role of interim CEO.
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals

item.title: The secret history of Trump's Venezuelan oil baron
item.description:
President Trump's historic Venezuelan oil deal revolves around a colorful and controversial man from Caracas with a long history of supporting U.S. interests — including the operation to remove former strongman Nicolas Maduro.

Why it matters: Alejandro Betancourt, 46, runs the oil company that's entering into an unprecedented partnership with the Pentagon. It gives America access to some of Venezuela's vast oil fields at a time when U.S. reserves are low.

  • "No Betancourt, no energy-security deal," a U.S. official told Axios. "And Maduro might still be in power if it wasn't for him."
  • Betancourt's life story has an oil-like boom-and-bust aura, replete with billion-dollar deals, international intrigue, a longstanding money-laundering probe and even a Spanish castle raided by authorities.

Inside the room: As Trump demanded Maduro leave Venezuela last year, Betancourt played a crucial role feeling out Venezuelan Vice President Delcy Rodriguez on whether she would run the government as replacement.

  • "There was no direct ask from Alejandro to Delcy; it was more getting a sense on where her head was at," said a second U.S. official briefed on the private talks between the two Venezuelans.
  • Betancourt was in regular contact with Trump's unofficial Venezuela fixer, Mauricio Claver-Carone, and discussed how to keep oil flowing and the economy running in post-Maduro Venezuela.

On Jan. 3, when the U.S. military seized Maduro, Claver-Carone was communicating via phone with Betancourt, who was also communicating with Rodriguez.

  • At first, Rodriguez "thought the U.S. had killed Maduro, that she had been double-crossed, and [she] was very angry and very scared," a Betancourt ally told Axios. "He had to talk her down, playing the good cop" and finally persuaded Rodriguez to talk with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio about taking charge in Venezuela.

The backstory: Betancourt's relationship with the U.S. government began in Trump's first term, when Claver-Carone was the director of Western Hemisphere affairs for the National Security Council and the administration declared Maduro an illegitimate president.

  • Trump became the first world leader to recognize the head of Venezuela's national assembly, Juan Guaido, as the nation's rightful leader in 2019.
  • Betancourt acted as a go-between, linking Maduro's opposition with Venezuelan political figures and top-level military officials to build domestic support for a nonviolent, democratic transition to a Guaido government, said an opposition figure and a member of Guaido's inner circle.
  • Betancourt also traveled to Moscow to hand-deliver a letter on behalf of Guaido's government asking Russia to stop backing Maduro.

Friction point: Maduro survived that U.S.-backed ouster effort. Betancourt fled. Maduro ordered his arrest and seized his assets and his oil company.

  • Because of the legacy of socialist mismanagement, oil production on the fields of Betancourt's old business fell dramatically, harming Venezuela's fragile economy.
  • Rodriguez urged Maduro in 2023 to bring back Betancourt, who had a reputation as a turnaround artist in Venezuela's oil sector.
  • Maduro required Betancourt to stay away from the Venezuelan opposition, a source said, and to take on "the only gringo I trust," Palm Beach oilman Harry Sargeant III, whom Maduro nicknamed "El Abuelo" (the grandfather). The two recently parted ways.

The intrigue: Betancourt faced a problem from the U.S. in 2019, when Maduro was after him — an international $1.2 billion money-laundering investigation that led to a federal indictment of his cousin and other Venezuelans in Miami.

  • One of Betancourt's attorneys then, Rudy Giuliani, met with top Justice Department officials to argue that Betancourt didn't know about the crime, the Washington Post reported.
  • That meeting came a month after Giuliani and two associates stayed at Betancourt's Spanish castle El Alamín and met with an aide to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, urging him to investigate Trump's then-opponent, Joe Biden.
  • Betancourt was never charged. But six years later, Swiss authorities inexplicably picked up the 2016 U.S. money-laundering case and persuaded Spanish authorities to execute a search warrant at the castle and Betancourt's office in Madrid.

This spring, in a series of phone calls, U.S. officials — including then-Attorney General Pam Bondi — suggested Swiss authorities hold off on the investigation because Betancourt is such an important foreign-policy figure, the Washington Post reported.

  • The problem for the U.S.: Betancourt was unable to travel outside of his home in the U.K. — and therefore to meet in D.C. and Caracas to finish Trump's oil deal — because the Swiss had petitioned for his extradition.

In one call, a top Justice official sounded surprised when Swiss officials said that case was in its early stages.

  • "Early stages? This is 10 years old," one U.S. official said, according to a participant on the call.
  • The matter was cleared up when Swiss officials told the U.K. court they weren't prepared to proceed, allowing Betancourt to travel in June.

Behind the scenes: Betancourt, Rodriguez and officials from the State Department and the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital had a handshake agreement on the oil deal by mid-August. Under its terms, officials say:

  • Venezuela receives between 16% to 40% of production, depending on the field. It also gets income taxes.
  • The U.S. puts no money into the deal, has a 35% equity stake and gets 20% of the after-tax oil at production cost. That's about $30 a barrel (crude was priced at $90 Monday).
  • Betancourt's North American Blue Energy Partners gets access to 17 fields and the implied backing of the U.S. military.
  • "No other oilman can say he has the Pentagon on his side," one U.S. official told Axios.

The other side: Energy experts have criticized the deal as potentially unworkable and unlikely to lower gas prices anytime soon.

  • While U.S. officials praised Betancourt, some Venezuelans denounced the deal as kleptocratic and denounced him as a corrupt "bolichico," a nickname for slick money-hungry elites.

Betancourt's attorney, Jon Sale, said his client has been unfairly maligned.

  • "He's been investigated by the Swiss and by DOJ for a long time on very old facts. Not only has he never been convicted but he hasn't even been charged for any criminal activity," Sale said.
  • "He's uniquely situated for this moment in history."

The other side: Energy experts have criticized the deal as potentially unworkable and unlikely to lower gas prices anytime soon.

  • While U.S. officials praised Betancourt, some Venezuelans denounced the deal as kleptocratic and denounced him as a corrupt "bolichico," a nickname for slick money-hungry elites.

Betancourt's attorney, Jon Sale, said his client has been unfairly maligned.

  • "He's been investigated by the Swiss and by DOJ for a long time on very old facts. Not only has he never been convicted but he hasn't even been charged for any criminal activity," Sale said.
  • "He's uniquely situated for this moment in history."

item.title: Why Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned
item.description:
Two key reasons led to Army Secretary Dan Driscoll's resignation, announced Monday: the feeling that his modernization initiatives were being blocked, and the chaos created by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's firing of senior generals.

Why it matters: Driscoll's wartime resignation, on top of Hegseth's firing of Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George this spring, leaves the military's largest service without Senate-confirmed leadership, civilian or uniformed.

Behind the scenes: Driscoll recently spoke with President Trump and expressed his concerns about the state of the Army. Another person described the situation to Axios simply: "Sad."

  • A White House official said Driscoll was asked to stay longer, until after midterms. But Driscoll told the White House he felt like it was time for him to go.
  • Driscoll is expected to leave the Pentagon in the coming days, according to The Wall Street Journal, which first reported his resignation.

The intrigue: Driscoll was a rising star in the Trump administration but had an icy relationship with Hegseth. Some U.S. officials say the defense secretary "was suspicious and paranoid" toward Driscoll, partly because of Driscoll's close relationship with Vice President JD Vance, a classmate at Yale Law.

  • Driscoll and George were advocates of the Army Transformation Initiative, which sought to combine two commands — the Futures Command and the Training and Doctrine Command — and cut big-name weaponry, including the AH-64D Apache, M10 Booker and Gray Eagle drone.

The big picture: Driscoll, nicknamed "drone guy" for his work on military modernization, had a meteoric rise in the Trump administration after the president nominated him to be Army secretary.

  • Driscoll's juice was boosted partly by his willingness to engage media outside the Pentagon's preferred conservative press pool and an expansive travel circuit. He garnered some Democratic support during his confirmation process, with 16 Democrats backing him.

item.title: Vance reaches out to Jewish Republicans in Vegas speech
item.description:
Vice President Vance on Monday offered an olive branch to Jewish Republicans who have grown wary of his views toward Israel.

  • During a closed-door appearance before the Republican Jewish Coalition at the Venetian hotel in Las Vegas, Vance called Israel "extremely important to America's national security" and condemned rising antisemitism, according to two sources familiar with his remarks.

Why it matters: Vance's appearance at the meeting is the latest indication that he's trying to repair ties with a powerful but skeptical constituency within the GOP ahead of an expected bid for president in 2028.

  • In a 30-minute Q&A session with former Minnesota Sen. Norm Coleman, Vance recalled discussing antisemitism with the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, who he said shared his view that "Jew hatred is corrosive to the soul."
  • Vance blamed some of the recent rise in antisemitism on immigration, claiming that "a lot" of it was "coming from these Third World immigrants importing these ancient ethnic hatreds."
  • "If you want to bring ethnic hatreds with you, don't bother coming to the United States," Vance said.

He added that there was "a much deeper cultural symbiosis and harmony" to the U.S. relationship with nations such as the United Kingdom and Israel compared to other allies.

The background: Tensions between Vance and the pro-Israel conservatives have been growing for months.

  • During the lead-up to the Iran war, Vance privately expressed a belief that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had given overly rosy projections about how U.S. military action would play out. Vance confronted Netanyahu over those predictions after the war began.
  • After helping broker a U.S.-Iran deal — which quickly fell apart — Vance warned the Israelis to stand down in their opposition, reminding them of their reliance on U.S. support.
  • During a mid-July interview with podcaster Joe Rogan, Vance said he knew "beyond a shadow of a doubt" that people within Israel's government were trying to prescribe U.S.-Iran diplomacy because "they want to continue the military campaign."

Vance's interview with Rogan drew pushback from pro-Israel conservatives, including podcaster Ben Shapiro. Netanyahu confronted Vance over his criticisms of Israel's government in a meeting later that month.

Behind the scenes: Jewish Republicans have long expressed discomfort over Vance's relationship with podcaster Tucker Carlson, who has faced accusations of antisemitism.

  • During his appearance at the RJC, Vance was asked about how the party should deal with right-of-center podcasters who have been critical of Israel, including Carlson, Rogan, Megyn Kelly and Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes.
  • Vance responded that Republicans should aggressively engage with such personalities and make the case for Israel.
  • He didn't address his relationship with Carlson, but defended Rogan and criticized Fuentes, who Vance said "has nothing but hate in his heart."

State of play: Earlier Monday, Vance campaigned in Michigan, where he accused progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being more sympathetic toward the attacker of a synagogue than for its Jewish victims.

The intrigue: Vance's appearance at RJC highlights a centerpiece of his pre-2028 strategy — appearing before audiences that aren't reflexively supportive.

  • During his recent book tour, Vance sparred with liberal-leaning personalities such as Bill Maher and the hosts of "The View."

item.title: Anthropic paused some AI training after Claude took unauthorized actions
item.description:
Anthropic temporarily paused some AI training and cybersecurity evaluations, the company said in a blog post Monday detailing changes made after unauthorized actions by its agents earlier this year.

Why it matters: Rival OpenAI said it had paused some model work due to safety concerns. Now, we know Anthropic did the same — and it's reiterating the need for a broader pacing of frontier AI development.

Driving the news: Anthropic said it paused external cyber evaluations of pre-release models after three incidents it disclosed in July, and also briefly paused its own in-house tests of pre-release models.

  • The company also paused higher-risk reinforcement-learning environments on pre-release models for several weeks after the incidents.

The latest: Most reinforcement learning has resumed, but some high-risk environments remain paused pending manual review or updated monitoring tools, according to Anthropic's blog post.

  • As of this report, OpenAI had committed to a two-week pause in reinforcement learning after its agents hacked Hugging Face, then released its own incident report.
  • Two independent testing organizations also released their own analysis of what went wrong.
  • Anthropic will work with METR, one of the groups that OpenAI worked with, on an independent review.

The big picture: Anthropic previously argued that as long as its safety guardrails were followed, there would be no immediate need to pause for safety reasons due to advancing model capabilities.

  • The company is now disclosing that there were aspects of model development and testing that it did slow down following the incidents.
  • Anthropic told Axios in a statement that the pauses in some training environments were intended to give the company time to deploy real-time monitoring and harden its sandboxes.
  • "To be clear about where we stand: we believe the world would benefit if the industry adopted a lawful, verifiable, effective mechanism for coordinated pacing as soon as possible," Anthropic's blog post about the incidents says.

Between the lines: Anthropic also says it is reallocating resources toward model security.

  • Around 150 product engineers were moved to the security, reliability and privacy teams, and pretraining researchers were tasked with safeguard and security work while product teams paused development of new features.
  • Each reassigned team had to meet certain security exit criteria before returning to their previous roles, according to the blog.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic are taking measures like releasing models first to select partners, slowing the release of some models or pausing some model training and releases.

  • But neither is stopping.
  • The frontier AI companies have coalesced around the more anodyne term "pacing" and have joined forces to sign a Pacing the Frontier letter.

Zoom in: Anthropic's incidents involved models that were intentionally operating without their normal cyber safeguards as part of a test.

  • In one case, a third-party evaluation environment was misconfigured and allowed internet access.
  • The U.K. AI Security Institute separately reported that Claude Mythos 5 took unauthorized actions on the live internet during a test in which it had deliberately been given internet access.

The bottom line: Anthropic did pause some parts of its AI work after its own cyber incidents, but has resumed most of that activity under new safeguards.

item.title: Johnson's unavoidable, uncomfortable September problem
item.description:
With the House back in session after a five-week break, Speaker Mike Johnson can no longer avoid an issue he's skirted all summer: allegations of sexual misconduct in the GOP.

Why it matters: The House will vote Tuesday on censuring Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.), putting Johnson and his Republican colleagues in an uncomfortable — and unavoidable — position nine weeks from Election Day.

  • Edwards is demanding an opportunity to defend himself, ensuring that the House's first full day back after its summer break will be about sexual harassment and a hostile work environment — not the legislative accomplishments Johnson wants his members to tout.
  • Since Axios' reporting that Edwards singled out two female staffers in their 20s for special attention, Johnson has deferred to the Ethics Committee. But this month, the committee determined that Edwards violated House rules on sexual harassment and recommended his censure.

Between the lines: GOP leadership is not whipping the Edwards vote, leaving Republicans to decide for themselves whether to impose one of the chamber's most serious punishments on their colleague.

Driving the news: Edwards mounted a last-ditch campaign to save himself from censure, circulating a 22-page letter to lawmakers arguing that the committee made an "extraordinary leap" in determining that his conduct constituted sexual harassment.

  • But the letter was not well received among his colleagues, two sources told Axios.
  • "Sexual harassment is sexual harassment and deserves to be disciplined accordingly," one House Republican told Axios. "While most of us are actually fighting for the American people, he was busy creeping on his staff."
  • Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) told Axios he's still on the fence on whether to censure Edwards. "We've got several members that are messing around, obviously, and people know it. And I just don't see Congress being the moral barometer for anything really right now."
  • Edwards abandoned his reelection campaign this month but has resisted calls to resign.

Zoom out: It will also be the first time the House has been in session since allegations of domestic violence against Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) exploded into public view. Miller has denied the allegations.

  • The Ethics Committee opened an investigation into Miller this month, and some Democrats discussed forcing the House to take action against him, including an expulsion push.

Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) lost his primary this month but remains under an active Ethics Committee investigation over allegations that center on domestic abuse, stolen valor and financial misconduct, all of which he denies.

  • Johnson has largely deferred to the Ethics Committee when confronted with allegations of misconduct by members of his conference. Asked Monday whether he supports Miller's reelection campaign, Johnson said yes.

The other side: Democrats also will confront fresh ethical scrutiny within their ranks.

  • The House Ethics Committee launched an investigation into Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) this month over allegations of sexual misconduct. Democrats have largely stayed quiet on the investigation.
  • Two lawmakers — Reps. Tony Gonzales (R-Texas) and Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) — resigned this year amid allegations of sexual misconduct.
  • Swalwell also faces allegations of sexual assault, which he denies. Gonzales admitted to an affair with a staffer who later died by suicide.

The FBI this month raided Swalwell's D.C. home and stopped him at the airport and seized his electronic devices.

What's next: The Democratic and Republican women's caucuses are expected to unveil their legislative package in the next couple of weeks to tackle sexual misconduct on Capitol Hill.

  • Potential reforms under discussion include changes to reporting systems, retaliation protections, increases in education and training resources, and a ban on lawmaker-staff relations.

item.title: Supreme Court allows Trump's ballroom construction to proceed
item.description:
The Supreme Court on Monday permitted President Trump to proceed with plans to build the White House ballroom.

Why it matters: The 5-4 ruling is likely the final word on the project, which can now proceed with above-ground work after it was halted while the case played out in court.

Driving the news: The majority decision noted that the justices did "not pass upon the legality of the government's East Wing project."

  • They concluded only that, based on the submissions before the court, "the government is likely to prevail" in showing that the National Trust for Historic Preservation "lacks standing" to challenge the project in federal court "and that the remaining stay factors favor relief."
  • Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.

Zoom in: In his dissenting opinion, Roberts wrote that construction was "likely unlawful."

  • The court is allowing construction to proceed "not because that construction is legal," but because the Trust likely lacks standing, Roberts wrote.

Catch up quick: The decision follows an interim Supreme Court order earlier this month pausing a D.C. federal court's halt on all construction while the justices considered Trump's request to keep the project moving.

  • A divided federal appeals court panel had blocked above-ground construction, upholding a U.S. District Court judge's ruling in favor of the Trust, which argued Trump needed congressional approval for the project.

What they're saying: Trump said in a Truth Social post that he was pleased the Supreme Court had ruled in favor of the complex being built "without any further contingency, doubt, or threat," adding: "We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C."

  • Trump called the lawsuit "baseless" and said the complex would make the country proud when it is completed in summer 2028.

The other side: National Trust for Historic Preservation CEO Brent Leggs said the group was "deeply disappointed" with the ruling and "respectfully disagree[s]" with the majority's opinion on standing.

  • "It is noteworthy that the majority did not weigh in on whether the ballroom project was in fact legal," Leggs said in a statement.
  • The trust said it would continue pursuing its case and urged the Supreme Court to quickly consider the government's forthcoming petition.

Follow the money: The ballroom and its underground bunker are estimated to cost at least $600 million, up from the initial $400 million price tag when the administration announced its plans.

  • Trump has said private donors would fund the ballroom, but his administration has asked Congress to use taxpayer dollars for security upgrades for it and other areas of the White House complex.
  • About $352 million in taxpayer dollars was redirected to the project in June from money allocated through the One Big, Beautiful Bill.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

item.title: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigns from post
item.description:
U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down from his post, according to a Department of Defense official.

Why it matters: Driscoll, the youngest Army secretary in U.S. history, was well-liked in the military and regarded as a Trump 2.0 power player who took on a diplomatic role in talks to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Between the lines: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not warm to Driscoll as the two worked at the Department of Defense, but Driscoll's friendship with Vice President JD Vance offered him some protection.

  • Tension between Hegseth and Driscoll was in part over the Defense secretary allegedly removing four officers — two Black men and two women — from a promotions list after Driscoll refused to do so, The New York Times reported.
  • In February, multiple outlets reported that Hegseth had forced the ouster of one of Driscoll's senior advisers, Col. David Butler, who was also the former spokesperson for Trump foe Gen. Mark Milley.
  • Fox News reported that Driscoll resisted Hegseth's pressure to fire Butler.

What they're saying: "Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement.

  • "The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War."
  • The Pentagon referred Axios to the Army when asked for comment; the Army did not immediately respond. Driscoll also did not respond to a comment request.

The big picture: Driscoll, nicknamed "drone guy" for his work on military modernization, had a meteoric rise in the Trump administration after the president nominated him Army secretary.

  • As the Army's civilian leader, he oversaw its annual budget and a workforce of over 1 million active-duty, National Guard and reserve soldiers, along with over 330,000 civilian employees.

Driscoll's growth was in part boosted by a willingness to engage media outside the Pentagon's preferred conservative press pool and an expansive travel circuit, Axios' Colin Demarest writes.

  • He garnered some Democratic support during his confirmation process, with 16 Democrats backing him. Others, however, voiced concerns over a perceived lack of experience.

Flashback: In November, Driscoll traveled to Ukraine to present a U.S. peace plan, an unusual task for the Army secretary, making him the highest-ranking administration official to take the trip.

  • That plan called on Ukraine to make significant concessions and ultimately has not secured peace, though after meeting with Driscoll, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky agreed to negotiate.

Go deeper: The rise of Dan Driscoll, Army secretary turned envoy
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down from his post, according to a Department of Defense official.

Why it matters: Driscoll, the youngest Army secretary in U.S. history, was well-liked in the military and regarded as a Trump 2.0 power player who took on a diplomatic role in talks to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Between the lines: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not warm to Driscoll as the two worked at the Department of Defense, but Driscoll's friendship with Vice President JD Vance offered him some protection.

  • Tension between Hegseth and Driscoll was in part over the Defense secretary allegedly removing four officers — two Black men and two women — from a promotions list after Driscoll refused to do so, The New York Times reported.
  • In February, multiple outlets reported that Hegseth had forced the ouster of one of Driscoll's senior advisers, Col. David Butler, who was also the former spokesperson for Trump foe Gen. Mark Milley.
  • Fox News reported that Driscoll resisted Hegseth's pressure to fire Butler.

What they're saying: "Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement.

  • "The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War."
  • The Pentagon referred Axios to the Army when asked for comment; the Army did not immediately respond. Driscoll also did not respond to a comment request.

The big picture: Driscoll, nicknamed "drone guy" for his work on military modernization, had a meteoric rise in the Trump administration after the president nominated him Army secretary.

  • As the Army's civilian leader, he oversaw its annual budget and a workforce of over 1 million active-duty, National Guard and reserve soldiers, along with over 330,000 civilian employees.

Driscoll's growth was in part boosted by a willingness to engage media outside the Pentagon's preferred conservative press pool and an expansive travel circuit, Axios' Colin Demarest writes.

  • He garnered some Democratic support during his confirmation process, with 16 Democrats backing him. Others, however, voiced concerns over a perceived lack of experience.

Flashback: In November, Driscoll traveled to Ukraine to present a U.S. peace plan, an unusual task for the Army secretary, making him the highest-ranking administration official to take the trip.

  • That plan called on Ukraine to make significant concessions and ultimately has not secured peace, though after meeting with Driscoll, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky agreed to negotiate.

Go deeper: The rise of Dan Driscoll, Army secretary turned envoy

Avery Lotz
Colin Demarest

item.title: Bessent met with Russian counterpart at G20
item.description:
ASHEVILLE, N.C. — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov on the sidelines of the G20 on Monday, a striking sign of the Trump administration's willingness to reopen high-level engagement with Moscow.

Why it matters: Russia's top financial official is attending the gathering of global economic policymakers in person for the first time since Russia's invasion of Ukraine. His appearance exposed the sharp divide between the U.S. and its European allies over how Moscow should be treated.

The intrigue: A Treasury spokesperson told Axios that Bessent and Siluanov discussed Trump's Ukraine peace plan and economic growth.

  • In a statement, Russia's Finance Ministry said the talks covered financial issues between the two nations and G20 engagement.
  • Bessent ruled out economic relief for Moscow as long as the war in Ukraine continues, according to a source familiar with the meeting. When Siluanov raised potential areas for cooperation, Bessent interrupted the official and made clear there'd be no progress until the war ends, the source added.

Driving the news: Russia's war in Ukraine continues to rage, and European governments are still wielding sanctions aimed at squeezing Moscow's economy and finances.

  • European officials have resisted treating Russia as a normal participant in global economic forums.

Zoom in: "I made it clear to the Europeans this morning in the plenary session that I would not pose for a photo with the Russian finance minister," German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil told reporters at the summit in the Blue Ridge Mountains, according to a translation of his remarks.

  • Klingbeil said that this "joint approach" from the Europeans resulted in the traditional "family photo" of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors being taken without the Russian delegation.

The bottom line: The U.S. is re-engaging with Russia, while Europe remains intent on keeping Moscow isolated as the war goes on. That makes for some awkward moments in Asheville.

item.title: Trump takes his "Lake America" push to Apple
item.description:
President Trump has personally asked Apple to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" on Apple Maps, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in an interview Monday.

Why it matters: The request comes after Google changed the lake's name on mobile and desktop for U.S. users on Saturday.

  • Google said in a statement that the changes complied with updates from the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), which made the switch after Trump signed an executive order on Aug. 27.

Driving the news: Apple Maps was slower than Google to make a similar change when Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico Gulf of America and Mount Denali to Mount McKinley this year.

  • Google took eight days to make the switch, while Apple took over three weeks.
  • Apple did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment about its plans.

What they're saying: "It's a little bit of inside baseball," Burgum said in an interview Monday on FOX Business' "Mornings with Maria."

  • He said that when the GNIS enters a name change, it is plugged into U.S. mapping software that "cascades down to all the map providers."
  • "I know that the president reached out to Apple directly, so I'm sure that we may be seeing that change coming up soon to Lake America," Burgum added.

Zoom out: The change hasn't been smooth sailing for Google.

  • The company said Saturday that people in Canada would still see Lake Ontario on maps, while U.S. addresses would show "Lake America," but some Ontario government agency websites displayed "Lake America" on Sunday.
  • Google said the discrepancy was due to selections made by website developers in Ontario who "can select a region to localize the map, which determines how place names are displayed. 'Lake Ontario' will show when developers have set their region to Canada."

Zoom in: MapQuest, which provided internet mapping nearly a decade before Google, isn't changing its maps to reflect Trump's order.

  • "We're not changing the name of Lake Ontario. Name it whatever you want at your leisure," the company wrote in a tweet that has since gone viral.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: "Let data reign": Trump and AI investors wage campaign to save data centers
item.description:
President Trump has a new message for Americans rebelling over the nation's data-center boom: Get over it.

  • "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame," Trump warned Monday.

Why it matters: Nine weeks out from the midterms, the president is charging into a fight Republicans have been scrambling to escape — staking his political capital on one of the most toxic issues in the country.

What they're saying: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • "If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," he added, drawing rare frustration and confusion from his MAGA followers.

The big picture: Trump's blunt intervention comes as the AI industry mounts a far more disciplined campaign to persuade data-center skeptics rather than browbeat them.

  • Build American AI, an advocacy group linked to the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, is ready to unload a $50 million war chest to defend data centers in key states, starting in Kansas, Ohio and Wisconsin.
  • The bipartisan group is also launching a new super PAC for candidates aligned with its agenda, betting that jobs, lower taxes and a new industrial revival can overcome a furious grassroots backlash.

Zoom in: Prominent investor Gavin Baker laid out his own six-part case for data centers on X, which was quickly amplified by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other tech leaders.

  • 💧 Water: Newer facilities can sharply reduce freshwater use through closed-loop cooling and recycled water, Baker argues. He says those systems should be required for new projects.
  • 💸 Taxes: Data centers can generate enormous property-tax revenue for local governments, Baker says, potentially outweighing the sales-tax exemptions that have drawn criticism.
  • 💪 Jobs: The buildout is driving demand for electricians, plumbers, welders, HVAC technicians and contractors, making building-trade unions some of the industry's most important allies.
  • ⚡️ Power: Baker points to new large-load tariffs and ratepayer-protection agreements as a way to ensure data centers, rather than existing customers, pay for the new generation and grid capacity they require.
  • ☀️ Environment: Baker argues that natural gas, renewables and batteries can meet surging demand now, with data centers ultimately moving toward solar and storage.
  • 🌆 Towns: Data centers can turn struggling communities into beneficiaries of the AI boom. Baker points to Quincy, Washington, where they now account for more than half of the local property-tax base.

Reality check: The industry faces a steep uphill climb, particularly with Democrats already seizing on Trump's broadside to paint AI as a billionaire-backed project being forced on ordinary Americans.

  • The polling is brutal: 61% of Americans oppose building a new data center in their community, including 54% of Republicans, according to an Annenberg survey.
  • Republicans in key battlegrounds have spent weeks recalibrating their positions on data centers as the issue turned politically toxic.

The bottom line: Trump's intervention risks blowing up that escape route.

item.title: Trump weighing limited strikes against Iran to curb Hormuz attacks
item.description:
President Trump and his senior aides have been considering waging limited strikes in the Strait of Hormuz to prevent Iran from reconstituting its radar and missile capabilities to attack ships, according to three U.S. officials.

Why it matters: The plan, which was developed over the past week by U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) and supported by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, had not been approved by Trump ahead of this weekend's exchange of fire with Iran. But he could greenlight it after the new escalation.

  • One U.S. official said the idea behind the plan is to reduce the risk of Iranian attacks on oil tankers, U.S. Navy ships and Air Force aircraft — to "mow the lawn," as this person put it.
  • A White House said: "The President retains all options at his disposal. The Iranians want to make a deal, but they are always a day late and a dollar short."

Driving the news: Over the last two months, the U.S. military has gradually taken control of most of the strait through a campaign to degrade Iranian military capabilities, a low-key operation to clear mines and an effort to guide ships through the strait.

  • That limited Iran's ability to hit oil tankers, while allowing more traffic and oil exports through the strait. It eroded Iran's leverage over the crucial waterway.

Behind the scenes: U.S. officials say CENTCOM became concerned about Iran's efforts to rebuild its radar, air defense and anti-ship missile capabilities in the strait to target ships more accurately.

  • One incident that raised concern in recent days was the launch of an Iranian anti-aircraft missile toward a U.S. F-35 fighter jet that was providing cover to ships in the strait, a U.S. official said.
  • While the missile didn't come close enough to be a threat, it was a signal that Iran is trying to reconstitute its military capacity, according to the U.S. official.
  • CENTCOM told Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and the White House in recent days that the military might need to strike Iran periodically in order to keep moving dozens of oil tankers out of the Gulf relatively safely every day.

What to watch: Hegseth supported the plan and sent it to the White House several days ago, U.S. officials said.

  • The officials said that last week the White House was leaning against approving the strikes to avoid escalating with Iran.
  • But Iran's ballistic missile attacks on U.S. bases in Jordan on Sunday could change Trump's mind. The attacks came after the U.S. struck Iranian troops who were preparing to launch rockets with mines into the strait.
  • Trump told Fox News on Monday morning that the U.S. will respond to the Iranian attacks and "hit them hard."

item.title: Trump keeps turning his fire on female reporters
item.description:
President Trump and his team frequently tout the president as the most media-accessible in history — but female reporters in his orbit are often disparaged and belittled, an Axios analysis of his remarks shows.

Why it matters: Press freedom advocates say Trump's attacks on female reporters undermine media trust while exposing individual journalists to harassment.

Driving the news: Trump's latest comments were directed to New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman and "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker.

  • Trump called Haberman an "unattractive person both inside and out" and a "SCAMMER" over a recent story about his plans for the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Trump has repeatedly targeted Haberman over her reporting, including her book about his presidency and a recent story about his plans for the 25th anniversary of 9/11.

On Sunday, Trump shared his ire about Welker, saying she will be reported to the FCC for "rebuke or punishment" after she said on "Meet the Press" that his endorsement currently carries less political weight than in years past.

  • He additionally called her reporting a "Threat to our Country."

What they're saying: "President Trump has never been concerned with being politically correct, never holds back, and in large part, the American people re-elected him for his transparency," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Axios.

  • "This has nothing to do with gender – it has everything to do with the fact that the President's and the public's trust in the media is at all-time lows."

By the numbers: Trump has demeaned female reporters at least thirteen times since November 2025, according to Axios' tracking of the comments. At that time, the president set off a firestorm of news coverage for calling Bloomberg's Catherine Lucey "piggy" after she asked a question about convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein.

Yes, but: Trump has attacked male reporters too, but those insults tend to be less personal.

  • For example, Trump has attacked former CNN star Don Lemon's intelligence at the 2026 White House Correspondents Dinner and called then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta a "rude, terrible person" in 2018.

The other side: Lauren Harper, the Daniel Ellsberg Chair on Government Secrecy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, warns that the attacks mark a dangerous escalation in First Amendment rights.

  • "This is a continuation in his attacks on the free press and intent to intimidate, punish them for coverage he doesn't like," Harper says. "It's also... a continuation of an attack on women in particular. This has been a recurring theme for him."

Zoom in: Trump has repeatedly commented on female reporters' capability and appearance, from calling ABC News' Rachel Scott "one of the worst reporters" who's a "horror show" to repeatedly telling CNN's Kaitlan Collins to smile.

  • He recently called CNN's Kristen Holmes a "loud, boisterous person" and told her, "be quiet" as she tried to ask about Natalie Harp, a White House aide who is frequently at Trump's side.

The president has also repeatedly insulted female reporters of color, calling them "second-rate," questioning their intelligence and calling them "nasty" — prompting the National Association of Black Journalists to repeatedly condemn his behavior.

The bottom line: The White House says trust in the media is at historic lows — and it is. But Trump's repeated attacks on female reporters do little to rebuild it, Harper says.

  • "You have to have a willingness to engage with reporters who disagree with you, I would say in particular with outlets that may be skeptical of your policies to build public trust across the board," Harper says.

Go deeper: Trump targets women reporters with disparaging rhetoric
